About this syllabus. This is the plan for the On-Demand (asynchronous) section of the course as designed. It is a one-semester course; you pace through the two quarters of your enrolled semester. Exact pacing and a few activities may vary from term to term. Your facilitator will confirm the specifics for your section.

COURSE OVERVIEW

Philosophy Honors is a one-semester survey of the Western philosophical tradition, opening with Socrates' search for moral and definitional knowledge in Plato's early dialogues, moving through the classical arguments for God's existence and the problem of evil, taking up the mind-body problem and the case for an immortal soul, and closing with two modules on the good life — one asking what makes a life good for the individual, the other asking what the good life requires of us together in political community. Each module tests its central question against real objections, and the course ends with a capstone Socratic dialogue synthesizing the philosophers studied across the term.

WHAT SCHOLARS WILL LEARN TO DO
  • Practice the Socratic method: define key terms precisely, test definitions against counterexamples, and follow an argument to its logical end.
  • Evaluate classical and modern arguments for God's existence, including Aquinas's Five Ways and the argument from design, alongside Hume's and Lewis's responses.
  • Explain the mind-body problem and compare substance dualism to materialist alternatives.
  • Analyze Plato's argument that the soul has three parts and its bearing on justice and the examined life.
  • Compare utilitarian, Kantian, and Aristotelian accounts of the good life and construct a reasoned defense of one.
  • Evaluate Hobbes's and Aristotle's competing accounts of why human beings form political communities.
  • Read primary philosophical texts closely and explain an argument's premises in your own words.
  • Construct and defend a reasoned philosophical position through writing and original dialogue.
BIG PROJECTS & MILESTONES

The course builds toward a capstone assessment at the close of each module. Target dates below follow a sample semester pacing; you pace to your own enrolled term, keeping each milestone roughly in order.

Reading Quizzes check that you did the reading. Weekly Warm-Ups are short writing exercises graded on a sincere, on-topic attempt rather than on polish. Assignments & Essays are graded closely against a rubric and are the main measure of your philosophical work in this course.

ON-DEMAND (ASYNCHRONOUS) LEARNING

In the On-Demand section you move through the course at your own pace within each quarter, guided by due dates that keep you on track. All assignments for a quarter open at its start and close at its end. Because the course is On-Demand, there is no grade penalty for missing an individual due date; any assignment not completed by the end of the quarter receives a zero, and assignments submitted in the final 14 days of a quarter receive a 10% deduction, so steady pacing matters.

Attendance is measured by assignment completion. Per school policy, a scholar who completes no assignment for ten consecutive school days, without notifying the school of an absence in advance, may be dropped from the course. Completion means a sincere attempt: real effort on real work. Rushed work, wrong or corrupted files, irrelevant or nonsense submissions, AI-generated filler, and word-salad responses do not count.

You are never on your own. A live facilitator grades your work, gives feedback, and hosts a weekly study hall and VR workshops.

USING AI IN THIS COURSE

Optima's AI policy does not ask whether a scholar used AI. It asks whether AI was used honestly, skillfully, and in a way that genuinely built your own thinking. AI may support your work, but it may not do the reasoning an assignment asks of you.

WHICH AI TOOLS YOU MAY USE
  • Every scholar. Any AI used for this course is school-controlled: tools built into Canvas assignments and into Optima's VR platform, set up to ask you questions and prompt your thinking rather than hand you answers. No assignment in this course requires a personal AI account.
  • Scholars under 14. Your facilitator may not ask, suggest, or require that you use an AI tool outside those school-controlled platforms. Your AI work for this course happens in Canvas and in VR.
  • Scholars 14 and older. Whether you use an outside AI tool for schoolwork is your family's decision, not the school's. It requires written parent or guardian permission on file with your facilitator, and your parent or guardian selects the tool, sets up the account, monitors it, and stays responsible for it. Optima does not provide, endorse, or manage personal AI accounts. Your facilitator's part is to judge whether the AI was used well.
WHAT IS EXPECTED WHEN YOU USE AI
  • Document it. Record the tool, the prompt you gave it, and the date. Using AI is not plagiarism. Turning in AI-generated work as entirely your own thought, with no documentation, is.
  • Verify it. AI states wrong things confidently, and you are responsible for every claim you submit, so check it against a credible source before it goes into your work. Verification is one of the skills this course grades.
  • Sound like yourself. Your work should read the way you write and speak in the rest of the course, take a real position rather than hedging, and be something you can explain on the spot, on camera or in VR, when your facilitator asks a follow-up question you did not expect.
  • Keep the process, not just the product. Prompt logs, drafts, revision notes, and VR recordings are gradeable evidence of your thinking. When an assignment asks for them, they count toward your grade.

Some assignments limit or exclude AI so that you build the underlying skill yourself, and the assignment page will say so. The reason is practical: you cannot judge whether an AI's answer is any good unless you can do the work without it.

LEARNING IN VIRTUAL REALITY

Optima is a virtual-reality school. Alongside your Canvas coursework, you will join immersive sessions on Optima's VR campus, where you meet teachers and fellow scholars, take part in live activities, and explore places and ideas you could not visit in an ordinary classroom. Keep your headset charged and ready for any scheduled VR sessions, and treat the VR campus with the same courtesy and seriousness you would a physical one. If you ever cannot get into VR for a session, tell your facilitator: there is an alternative way to take part so you do not fall behind.

BEING AN OPTIMA SCHOLAR

Optima's mission is an excellent, virtue-centered education, and virtue is at the center of this course as much as any other. Every scholar is expected to practice the seven virtues that shape life at Optima: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. In practice that means: do your own honest work; treat everyone you meet in, through, or because of this course with respect, in writing, in discussion, and in VR; engage actively rather than passively; come to office hours to get help, meet other scholars, and get to know your facilitator; and take responsibility for your own pacing and progress. You belong to a house and a community of scholars, not only to a course.

WHAT YOU NEED & STAYING CONNECTED
  • ☐ A computer with reliable internet and access to Canvas.
  • ☐ A VR headset, charged and ready for scheduled immersive sessions.
  • ☐ Microsoft 365 (Word, PowerPoint) with OneDrive, for documents you create and submit.
  • ☐ A notebook or binder, and pens or pencils, for reading notes and primary source work.

Staying connected. Updates about this course are posted on the course's Canvas page; school-wide updates are posted in your Homeroom Canvas course. Check both regularly. Your facilitator holds office hours and is glad to help with the material, to meet you, or to talk through your plans: come by, or reach out any time by email.

About this syllabus. This is the plan for the On-Demand (asynchronous) section of the course as designed. It is a one-semester course; you pace through the two quarters of your enrolled semester. Exact pacing and a few activities may vary from term to term. Your facilitator will confirm the specifics for your section.

COURSE OVERVIEW

Philosophy Honors is a one-semester survey of the Western philosophical tradition, opening with Socrates' search for moral and definitional knowledge in Plato's early dialogues, moving through the classical arguments for God's existence and the problem of evil, taking up the mind-body problem and the case for an immortal soul, and closing with two modules on the good life — one asking what makes a life good for the individual, the other asking what the good life requires of us together in political community. Each module tests its central question against real objections, and the course ends with a capstone Socratic dialogue synthesizing the philosophers studied across the term.

Each week pairs a short reading quiz with a brief written warm-up applying that week's idea to a real question or text, and each module closes with a substantive capstone essay or dialogue that puts the whole module's argument to work.

WHAT SCHOLARS WILL LEARN TO DO
  • Practice the Socratic method: define key terms precisely, test definitions against counterexamples, and follow an argument to its logical end.
  • Evaluate classical and modern arguments for God's existence, including Aquinas's Five Ways and the argument from design, alongside Hume's and Lewis's responses.
  • Explain the mind-body problem and compare substance dualism to materialist alternatives.
  • Analyze Plato's argument that the soul has three parts and its bearing on justice and the examined life.
  • Compare utilitarian, Kantian, and Aristotelian accounts of the good life and construct a reasoned defense of one.
  • Evaluate Hobbes's and Aristotle's competing accounts of why human beings form political communities.
  • Read primary philosophical texts closely and explain an argument's premises in your own words.
  • Construct and defend a reasoned philosophical position through writing and original dialogue.
BIG PROJECTS & MILESTONES

The course builds toward a capstone assessment at the close of each module. Target dates below follow a sample semester pacing; you pace to your own enrolled term, keeping each milestone roughly in order.

Reading Quizzes check that you did the reading. Weekly Warm-Ups are short writing exercises graded on a sincere, on-topic attempt rather than on polish. Assignments & Essays are graded closely against a rubric and are the main measure of your philosophical work in this course.

ON-DEMAND (ASYNCHRONOUS) LEARNING

In the On-Demand section you move through the course at your own pace within each quarter, guided by due dates that keep you on track. All assignments for a quarter open at its start and close at its end. Because the course is On-Demand, there is no grade penalty for missing an individual due date; any assignment not completed by the end of the quarter receives a zero, and assignments submitted in the final 14 days of a quarter receive a 10% deduction, so steady pacing matters.

Attendance is measured by assignment completion. Per school policy, a scholar who completes no assignment for ten consecutive school days, without notifying the school of an absence in advance, may be dropped from the course. Completion means a sincere attempt: real effort on real work. Rushed work, wrong or corrupted files, irrelevant or nonsense submissions, AI-generated filler, and word-salad responses do not count.

You are never on your own. A live facilitator grades your work, gives feedback, and hosts a weekly study hall and VR workshops.

USING AI IN THIS COURSE

Optima's AI policy does not ask whether a scholar used AI. It asks whether AI was used honestly, skillfully, and in a way that genuinely built your own thinking. AI may support your work, but it may not do the reasoning an assignment asks of you.

WHICH AI TOOLS YOU MAY USE
  • Every scholar. Any AI used for this course is school-controlled: tools built into Canvas assignments and into Optima's VR platform, set up to ask you questions and prompt your thinking rather than hand you answers. No assignment in this course requires a personal AI account.
  • Scholars under 14. Your facilitator may not ask, suggest, or require that you use an AI tool outside those school-controlled platforms. Your AI work for this course happens in Canvas and in VR.
  • Scholars 14 and older. Whether you use an outside AI tool for schoolwork is your family's decision, not the school's. It requires written parent or guardian permission on file with your facilitator, and your parent or guardian selects the tool, sets up the account, monitors it, and stays responsible for it. Optima does not provide, endorse, or manage personal AI accounts. Your facilitator's part is to judge whether the AI was used well.
WHAT IS EXPECTED WHEN YOU USE AI
  • Document it. Record the tool, the prompt you gave it, and the date. Using AI is not plagiarism. Turning in AI-generated work as entirely your own thought, with no documentation, is.
  • Verify it. AI states wrong things confidently, and you are responsible for every claim you submit, so check it against a credible source before it goes into your work. Verification is one of the skills this course grades.
  • Sound like yourself. Your work should read the way you write and speak in the rest of the course, take a real position rather than hedging, and be something you can explain on the spot, on camera or in VR, when your facilitator asks a follow-up question you did not expect.
  • Keep the process, not just the product. Prompt logs, drafts, revision notes, and VR recordings are gradeable evidence of your thinking. When an assignment asks for them, they count toward your grade.

Some assignments limit or exclude AI so that you build the underlying skill yourself, and the assignment page will say so. The reason is practical: you cannot judge whether an AI's answer is any good unless you can do the work without it.

LEARNING IN VIRTUAL REALITY

Optima is a virtual-reality school. Alongside your Canvas coursework, you will join immersive sessions on Optima's VR campus, where you meet teachers and fellow scholars, take part in live activities, and explore places and ideas you could not visit in an ordinary classroom. Keep your headset charged and ready for any scheduled VR sessions, and treat the VR campus with the same courtesy and seriousness you would a physical one. If you ever cannot get into VR for a session, tell your facilitator: there is an alternative way to take part so you do not fall behind.

BEING AN OPTIMA SCHOLAR

Optima's mission is an excellent, virtue-centered education, and virtue is at the center of this course as much as any other. Every scholar is expected to practice the seven virtues that shape life at Optima: courage, courtesy, honesty, perseverance, self-government, service, and responsibility. In practice that means: do your own honest work; treat everyone you meet in, through, or because of this course with respect, in writing, in discussion, and in VR; engage actively rather than passively; come to office hours to get help, meet other scholars, and get to know your facilitator; and take responsibility for your own pacing and progress. You belong to a house and a community of scholars, not only to a course.

WHAT YOU NEED & STAYING CONNECTED
  • ☐ A computer with reliable internet and access to Canvas.
  • ☐ A VR headset, charged and ready for scheduled immersive sessions.
  • ☐ Microsoft 365 (Word, PowerPoint) with OneDrive, for documents you create and submit.
  • ☐ A notebook or binder, and pens or pencils, for reading notes and primary source work.

Staying connected. Updates about this course are posted on the course's Canvas page; school-wide updates are posted in your Homeroom Canvas course. Check both regularly. Your facilitator holds office hours and is glad to help with the material, to meet you, or to talk through your plans: come by, or reach out any time by email.

A Conversation Worth Having
Assignment · 20 pts
📖 READING FOCUS
Apology
Plato
Socrates claims that the unexamined life is not worth living, a claim easy to agree with in the abstract and hard to act on in particular. This warm-up asks you to stage a small, real version of the examination he describes.
Paired with: Lesson 1c · The Unexamined Life and the Purpose of Philosophy
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write a short original dialogue, 150–250 words, in which one character states a plan or value they have never questioned, and a second speaker asks one genuine question that opens it up. No resolution is required; Socrates rarely gets one either.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What does it take for a life, or even a single belief, to count as “examined”?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Set the scene. A specific, ordinary moment: a hallway, a car ride, a text exchange. Keep it concrete.
2
State the unexamined assumption. One character says something they believe confidently and have never really tested.
3
Ask one real question. The second speaker asks a single question that unsettles the assumption, without lecturing or resolving it.
4
End honestly. Do not tie it up. An unresolved ending is a correct ending here.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The assumption is stated with genuine confidence, not set up as an obvious strawman.
☐
The question is a real question, not a disguised argument or a gotcha.
☐
Both voices sound like people, not mouthpieces.
☐
The dialogue connects, explicitly or implicitly, to the idea of the examined life.
📊 HOW THIS IS SCORED
Complete (20 pts): A sincere attempt: real effort on real work, following the directions above.
Incomplete (0 pts): Not submitted, or not a sincere attempt. Rushed work, off-topic or nonsense submissions, and effort-free filler do not count as complete.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Week 1 Warm-Up: A Conversation Worth Having
Submit as a Word document, PDF, or typed directly into the Canvas text entry box. 150–250 words.
Due: End of Week 1
This is a warm-up, not the Module 1 Capstone: keep it short, keep it honest, and do not feel obligated to solve anything. You will get a full dialogue assignment later in this module.

Journal Entry: Your Own Euthyphro
Assignment · 20 pts
📖 READING FOCUS
Euthyphro
Plato
At the beginning of the Euthyphro, Socrates notices that Euthyphro is using the word pious with great confidence to justify a serious and controversial action, and asks what that word actually means: not an example of it, but the principle that makes all pious acts pious. Euthyphro cannot do it, and the inability turns out to matter. This assignment asks you to do what Socrates did, starting from your own world.
Paired with: Lesson 2c · The Euthyphro Dilemma
📋 ASSIGNMENT OVERVIEW
Write a journal entry of 600–800 words in which you identify a concept that people around you, in conversation, in argument, online, at home, on a team, in a classroom, use to justify actions or positions, and then subject that concept to the kind of examination Socrates applies to piety in the Euthyphro.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What concept do people in your life use to justify their actions, and does it actually hold up once you test it the way Socrates tests Euthyphro's definitions?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Identify the concept. Choose a word or short phrase people in your life invoke when justifying something, a term of justification, not mere description, the way pious functions for Euthyphro. Some possibilities, only to get you thinking: fair, respectful, toxic, brave, loyal, authentic, earned, safe, honest, mature. The best choice is a word you have actually heard recently, in a real context that mattered.
2
Show the concept at work. Describe a specific instance, a conversation, an argument you witnessed, a post you read, a decision explained to you, in which someone used this concept to justify something. What was being justified, and what was the word doing in that justification? Be concrete.
3
Extract the definition. State the underlying principle explicitly, in the form Socrates is always after: The [concept] is [what]. In the Euthyphro, Euthyphro's working definition turns out to be something like the pious is whatever the gods love, though he never quite says this until Socrates draws it out of him. Do the same: find the implicit definition actually powering the justification in Step 2.
4
Test the definition. Use two tools. The counterexample: find a case where the definition would apply but the concept clearly should not, or vice versa. The circularity test: does the definition actually tell you what the concept is, or does it smuggle the concept back in, the way "the pious is what all the gods love" ultimately reduces to "the gods love the pious because it is pious"? You do not need to solve the problem. Socrates never does. Show that the definition, as stated, does not hold, and say clearly what the difficulty is.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The concept is genuinely in use in your world and functions as a term of justification, not mere description.
☐
The example is specific and concrete enough that the definition can be extracted from it.
☐
The definition is genuinely implicit in the example, drawn out rather than invented, and stated clearly and testably.
☐
The test is a real argument: a counterexample that actually damages the definition, or a circularity that actually exposes a problem.
☐
The entry contains at least one direct, substantive reference to the Euthyphro by Stephanus number.
📊 GRADING RUBRIC
Criteria Excellent (5) Proficient (4) Developing (2–3) Beginning (0–1) Pts
Concept Identified
5 pts		 A real, currently-used term of justification, sharply chosen A genuine justificatory term, if a bit generic Leans descriptive rather than justificatory Not a term of justification at all 5 pts
Concept Shown at Work
5 pts		 Specific, concrete example a definition can be drawn from Clear example, somewhat general Vague or secondhand example No real example given 5 pts
Definition Extracted
5 pts		 Genuinely drawn from the example, clear and testable Reasonably drawn out, mostly testable Vague or only loosely connected to the example No definition actually stated 5 pts
Definition Tested
5 pts		 A real counterexample or circularity that damages the definition, plus a substantive Stephanus-cited connection to the text A workable test and a genuine, if brief, textual connection Test is weak or the textual connection is decorative No real test attempted; no textual connection 5 pts
Total: 20 pts
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS
Canvas Assignment Name: Week 2 Journal: Your Own Euthyphro
Submit as a Word document, PDF, or typed directly into the Canvas text entry box. 600–800 words.
Due: End of Week 2

Writing a Philosophical Dialogue
Assignment · 100 pts
📖 PURPOSE
Plato's dialogues begin with ordinary conversations that gradually develop into careful philosophical inquiry. This assignment asks you to imitate Plato's literary and philosophical method by transforming an everyday conversation into a sustained investigation of a significant philosophical question. Writing a philosophical dialogue is not the same as writing a scene in which two characters exchange opinions. It requires genuine philosophical work: identifying a concept, subjecting it to the kinds of tests Socrates applies in the Euthyphro and the Meno, following the argument wherever it leads, and letting the conversation end honestly, which may mean ending in aporia rather than a tidy conclusion.
🎯 THE ASSIGNMENT
Write an original philosophical dialogue featuring Socrates as one speaker and an ordinary contemporary person as the other. Length: 800-1,200 words of dialogue.
📋 SETTING AND TOPIC
Your other speaker can be an Optima student, a neighbor, a family member, or any character who would plausibly encounter Socrates in an everyday setting: a hallway after class, a lunch table, a sports practice, a coffee shop. The philosophical conversation should arise naturally from ordinary circumstances rather than appearing out of nowhere.
Through questioning rather than lecturing, Socrates should lead the conversation toward a careful examination of a genuine philosophical issue: justice, courage, friendship, beauty, knowledge, truth, honesty, loyalty, fairness, or the meaning of a life well lived, among other possibilities. The best topics are concepts your other character would plausibly care about and feel confident about before Socrates starts asking questions. You are not limited to this list if a different concept is genuinely in play in your own life and can sustain the kind of examination the Euthyphro and the Meno demonstrate.
📝 THE STRUCTURE OF THE DIALOGUE
1
The Occasion. Something in the setting prompts a confident claim or assumption from the non-Socratic character. Socrates notices it and asks about it.
2
First Definition and Refutation. Socrates asks for a definition of the key concept. The character gives one. Socrates examines it using the Euthyphro's methods: is it a principle or merely an example? Does it generate contradictions? Does it give the essence rather than an accompanying attribute? The first definition should fail.
3
Continued Inquiry. The character tries at least one more definition. Socrates examines it in the same spirit. This phase is where the philosophical substance of your dialogue lives; the examination should reveal something genuinely interesting.
4
Aporia or Provisional Conclusion. The dialogue ends honestly, in genuine puzzlement or a tentative answer both speakers recognize as incomplete. What is not appropriate is an artificially neat resolution in which Socrates supplies the answer and the character gratefully accepts it. Plato's dialogues do not end that way, and neither should yours.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
Socrates uses questions throughout, never simply lectures or tells the character the answer.
☐
Each definition actually fails for a genuine reason: a real counterexample or a real contradiction, not a forced or unfair refutation.
☐
Both characters sound like real people; the setting is specific and the turn to philosophy feels natural.
☐
At least one moment explicitly or implicitly connects to the Apology, the Euthyphro, or the Meno, by borrowing a logical move, echoing an argument, or having the character reference something they've heard about Socrates.
☐
The dialogue ends in genuine aporia or an honestly provisional conclusion, not an artificially tidy resolution.
📤 SUBMISSION INSTRUCTIONS

Submit as a Word document, PDF, or typed directly into the Canvas text entry box. 800-1,200 words of dialogue.
Due: End of Week 4
This is not a scene from a play or a debate. In a scene, the dialogue serves character and plot; here, the dialogue must serve the argument. In a debate, both sides argue from predetermined positions; here, both speakers are genuinely trying to find out what is true. The character who ends the dialogue confused but curious has participated in something more valuable than the character who ends it having been defeated.

Module 2 Capstone
Aquinas and the Five Ways
Assignment · 25 pts
📖 OVERVIEW
In Question 2, Article 3 of the Summa Theologica (Freddoso translation), Thomas Aquinas offers five distinct arguments for the existence of God. Each begins from something observable in the world, motion, causation, contingency, degrees of perfection, or purposive order, and reasons from that observation to a first cause, which Aquinas identifies as God. Your assignment is to select one of these five arguments, lay out its logical structure carefully, and then either mount a sustained challenge to it or construct a defense of it against a serious objection. The goal is not to express a personal opinion about God, but to practice argument analysis: identifying premises, evaluating whether they hold, and reasoning carefully about what follows.
📋 THE FIVE WAYS AT A GLANCE
Way Starting point Core claim
1st Motion / change Everything moved is moved by another; infinite regress is impossible; therefore a first, unmoved mover.
2nd Efficient causation Nothing is its own cause; a causal chain cannot regress infinitely; therefore a first uncaused cause.
3rd Contingency Some things can exist or not; if everything were contingent, nothing would exist now; therefore something exists necessarily.
4th Degrees of perfection Gradations of goodness, truth, and being imply a maximum, which causes all others in that genus.
5th Governance / teleology Non-cognitive bodies act consistently toward ends; this requires direction by an intelligent being.
Use this table for orientation only. Your essay must work from the text itself. The First, Second, and Fifth Ways are the most structurally transparent starting points; the Third Way is subtle and easy to misread; the Fourth relies on an Aristotelian premise about causation. Choosing a harder Way is not rewarded with higher marks, but genuinely engaging with it is.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Does your chosen Way's argument actually establish its conclusion, or does a specific premise fail to hold up under pressure?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Identify your Way and state its conclusion. Name the Way you have chosen and state, in one or two sentences, what Aquinas concludes at the end of it. Do not summarize the argument yet, just name the destination.
2
Lay out the argument's premises. Identify and number each distinct premise Aquinas relies on. A "premise" is a claim the argument assumes or asserts as a step toward the conclusion. Aquinas's arguments typically have two or three load-bearing premises; do not inflate the list. This is the most careful and deliberate part of your essay.
3
State your thesis. In one sentence, state whether you will challenge or defend the argument, and identify which premise or move your essay will focus on. Example (challenge): "I will challenge the First Way by arguing that its claim that an infinite regress of movers is impossible is not adequately supported." Example (defense): "I will defend the Fifth Way against the objection that evolutionary processes can explain goal-directedness without invoking an intelligent director."
4
Develop your argument. If challenging: identify the weakest premise, state your objection with a reason or example, and consider the strongest reply Aquinas or his defenders might give, then respond to it. If defending: identify a serious objection targeting a specific premise, state or construct Aquinas's reply, and explain where the defense succeeds and where it remains incomplete. An essay that ignores the best counterargument is not a philosophical essay.
5
Conclude. In two to four sentences, state what your essay has shown and what remains genuinely open. You are not required to resolve everything; honesty about remaining difficulty is philosophically appropriate.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
All load-bearing premises are identified, numbered, and stated in your own words, not lifted directly from the text.
☐
Aquinas's argument is represented faithfully, with at least two direct quotations or close paraphrases cited by article.
☐
Your objection or defense targets a specific premise, not the conclusion in general, and addresses the strongest counterargument.
☐
The essay follows the required structure, states a clear thesis, and is precise and easy to follow.

The Good Life: A Philosophical Defense
Assignment · 25 pts
📖 OVERVIEW
Module 4 has followed a single question through four different philosophical traditions: what is the good life? Plato answers in terms of the just soul; Mill in terms of happiness; Kant in terms of the good will; Aristotle in terms of eudaimonia. These are genuinely different accounts, grounded in different assumptions about reason, community, and what makes a life worth living, and they disagree with each other sharply. For this assignment, you will enter that disagreement as a participant, not a spectator: choose one account, defend it, and confront its strongest objection honestly.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
What makes a human life genuinely good, and does your chosen account survive its strongest objection?
📋 CHOOSE ONE ACCOUNT TO DEFEND
Plato — the just life, a well-ordered soul in which reason governs appetite, is better than the unjust life regardless of external circumstances. Strongest objection: Glaucon's Ring of Gyges. Does the soul's internal harmony answer this, or does it depend on external goods Glaucon has already stripped away?
Mill — the good life is genuine happiness: active engagement with higher pleasures and real contribution to others' welfare. Strongest objection: utilitarianism seems to permit sacrificing an individual's interests for aggregate benefit. Does Mill's account of justice, or his higher-pleasures distinction, adequately protect individuals?
Kant — the good life is governed by the moral law: acting from duty, respecting every person's dignity. Strongest objection: this account is psychologically cold, excluding love and friendship from what gives an action genuine moral worth. Does it leave room for a fully human life, or does it demand something inhuman?
Aristotle — the good life is eudaimonia: the excellent activity of a person of good character, living in community, over a complete life. Strongest objection: this account depends on contingent goods (health, community, resources) outside a person's control. Can it explain why justice is unconditionally required, or does it collapse into "good for people like you, in circumstances like yours"?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
State a position. Choose one of the four accounts and defend it as the most persuasive answer to what makes a life genuinely good.
2
Explain the account precisely enough to distinguish it from the other three. What does it say the good life consists in? What argument supports it?
3
Raise the strongest objection to your account, from the module or of your own devising. State it as charitably and forcefully as you can.
4
Respond to the objection. Can your account absorb it, modify itself, or show that it misses the mark? Support your response with reasoning, not assertion.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
A clear, specific thesis is stated early and maintained throughout the essay.
☐
The chosen account is explained accurately and distinctively, not conflated with the other three.
☐
The objection is stated precisely, charitably, and at the account's most vulnerable point.
☐
The response engages the objection directly, showing how the account absorbs, answers, or reframes it.
☐
At least two texts from Module 4 are cited by author and work, woven into the argument rather than dropped in mechanically.

The Socratic Dialogue
Assignment · 30 pts
📖 OVERVIEW
This is the culminating project of the course. Write an original philosophical dialogue, a conversation between a Socratic figure and a fictional interlocutor, that begins with an ordinary everyday issue and presses it, through philosophical questioning, toward a deep question this course has equipped you to engage. You have spent a semester learning to ask for definitions, test them, follow arguments where they lead, and hold difficult questions with patience and honesty. This assignment asks you to practice it yourself, in your own voice, rather than only following along when Plato or Aristotle does it.
🎯 FOCUS QUESTION
Can you take an ordinary disagreement and, through genuine question-and-answer, press it toward one of philosophy's deepest and oldest questions?
📝 STUDENT DIRECTIONS
1
Feature a Socratic questioner (who may but need not be named Socrates) who drives the conversation through question-and-answer, modeling genuine curiosity, a willingness to follow the argument wherever it leads, and honesty about what they do and do not know.
2
Feature a thoughtful interlocutor, a fictional character who holds a view worth examining, gives real intelligent responses, and pushes back rather than walking into obvious traps.
3
Begin with an everyday issue, something concrete and recognizable, and let the questioning carry the conversation to a deep philosophical question: what is justice, in a soul, in a community, or both; what does it mean to live well; why do we need political authority; is there an objective good; what kind of thing are you, and why does it matter.
4
Reach genuine philosophical depth: at least one definition or position that can be examined and tested, at least one serious objection or counterexample, and a demonstration that the question is harder than it first appeared.
5
End in aporia or partial insight, not a tidy resolution. Genuine puzzlement that is richer and more honest than the confident-but-shallow position the interlocutor started with is philosophically appropriate and often more honest than a neat ending.
💬 A SAMPLE OPENING (TO ILLUSTRATE THE STYLE; DO NOT COPY)
Alex: You know what frustrates me? My sister broke the rules of the game, and everyone just let it slide because she's younger. It's not fair.

Jordan: What do you mean, "not fair"?

Alex: She got away with something the rest of us don't get away with. Different rules for different people.

Jordan: Is that always unfair? Or only sometimes?

Alex: If the rules are the same for everyone, it's fair. If they're not, it isn't.

Jordan: But we have all kinds of rules that treat people differently, different speed limits in school zones, different voting ages, different sentencing guidelines for adults and children. Are all of those unfair?

Alex: ...I guess not all different treatment is unfair.

Jordan: So what makes the difference? When is treating people differently just, and when is it unjust?
From here the dialogue could develop toward Aristotle's view that justice is treating equals equally and unequals unequally (but what makes people equal?), toward Plato's account of justice as each part doing its own work, toward Hobbes's view that justice just is whatever the sovereign commands, and so on.
✅ SUCCESS CRITERIA
☐
The Socratic questioner asks short, focused questions rather than giving speeches.
☐
The interlocutor gives genuine, considered replies and pushes back at least once.
☐
The dialogue has a clear philosophical arc, moving from an everyday issue to a genuine deep question, even if it ends in productive confusion.
☐
At least one concept, argument, or distinction from the course is accurately and naturally integrated, not name-dropped.
☐
The dialogue sounds like real people talking, not a philosophy textbook read aloud.

quizzes.title: Week 1 Reading Quiz: Plato's Apology
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Plato's Apology.

questions.text: Socrates is brought to trial on two formal charges. What are they?

answers.text: Impiety toward the gods of the city and corruption of the youth of Athens
Treason against Athens and association with the Thirty Tyrants
Charging fees for instruction and practicing sorcery
Teaching foreigners and refusing military service

questions.feedback_correct: The formal accusation, as Socrates recounts it, is that he fails to acknowledge the gods that Athens acknowledges, introduces new divine beings, and corrupts the young. Socrates argues that beneath these formal charges lies a deeper, older prejudice shaped partly by Aristophanes' satirical portrayal of him in The Clouds.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The formal accusation, as Socrates recounts it, is that he fails to acknowledge the gods that Athens acknowledges, introduces new divine beings, and corrupts the young. Socrates argues that beneath these formal charges lies a deeper, older prejudice shaped partly by Aristophanes' satirical portrayal of him in The Clouds.

questions.text: What did the oracle at Delphi say when Socrates' friend Chaerephon asked about him?

answers.text: That Socrates should leave Athens before his enemies could harm him
That Socrates was the most impious man in Greece
That Socrates would be remembered for ten thousand years
That no one was wiser than Socrates

questions.feedback_correct: Chaerephon asked the oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the Pythia replied: no one. Socrates found this puzzling, since he was convinced he possessed no significant wisdom, and the puzzle drove him to undertake the investigation of Athenian reputations that defined the rest of his life.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Chaerephon asked the oracle whether anyone was wiser than Socrates, and the Pythia replied: no one. Socrates found this puzzling, since he was convinced he possessed no significant wisdom, and the puzzle drove him to undertake the investigation of Athenian reputations that defined the rest of his life.

questions.text: After examining the politicians of Athens, what conclusion does Socrates reach about them?

answers.text: They are genuinely wise but refuse to share their wisdom with ordinary citizens
They know nothing worth knowing, and unlike Socrates, they do not know that they know nothing
They are wise in matters of governance but ignorant about philosophy
They are wise but jealous of Socrates' reputation, which is why they persecute him

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates finds that the politicians believe themselves to be wise when they are not. His own advantage, he concludes, is "this small extent: that I do not think I know what I do not know." (Apology, 21d) The gap between actual and believed knowledge is exactly the deficiency Socratic examination is designed to expose.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Socrates finds that the politicians believe themselves to be wise when they are not. His own advantage, he concludes, is "this small extent: that I do not think I know what I do not know." (Apology, 21d) The gap between actual and believed knowledge is exactly the deficiency Socratic examination is designed to expose.

questions.text: Socrates compares himself to a gadfly and Athens to a large, noble horse. What is the point of this comparison?

answers.text: That Socrates is quick and difficult to catch, and Athens is slow to understand
That Socrates is small and weak compared to the power of the city
That a great city easily becomes complacent, and Socrates' role is to sting it into wakefulness
That Socrates admires Athens the way one admires a fine animal, even if it is dangerous

questions.feedback_correct: The gadfly image is about the function of honest questioning in civic life. A large horse can become inert and sluggish without something to rouse it; a city whose leaders cannot define justice, whose generals cannot define courage, and whose poets cannot explain what they mean is similarly in danger of a self-satisfied decline. Socrates sees his uncomfortable, enemy-making questioning as a service the city requires.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The gadfly image is about the function of honest questioning in civic life. A large horse can become inert and sluggish without something to rouse it; a city whose leaders cannot define justice, whose generals cannot define courage, and whose poets cannot explain what they mean is similarly in danger of a self-satisfied decline. Socrates sees his uncomfortable, enemy-making questioning as a service the city requires.

questions.text: When the jury convicts him and Socrates must propose an alternative punishment, what does he initially suggest?

answers.text: That he be given free meals at the Prytaneum, the honor given to Olympic victors
That he be exiled from Athens permanently
That he be fined one hundred drachmas
That he be imprisoned for five years and then released

questions.feedback_correct: In a passage that many of his jurors apparently found infuriating, Socrates argues that his service to Athens has been greater than that of the athletes honored at the Prytaneum. Athletes make people feel good; Socrates has tried to make them actually good. He eventually settles on a small fine, but the damage to the jury's mood was done. The death penalty was voted by a wider margin than the original conviction.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In a passage that many of his jurors apparently found infuriating, Socrates argues that his service to Athens has been greater than that of the athletes honored at the Prytaneum. Athletes make people feel good; Socrates has tried to make them actually good. He eventually settles on a small fine, but the damage to the jury's mood was done. The death penalty was voted by a wider margin than the original conviction.

questions.text: What does Socrates say is the greatest good available to a human being, and what famous claim does he make about an unexamined life?

answers.text: The greatest good is health, and a man who neglects his body has nothing; he says nothing about the examined life
The greatest good is friendship with the gods; he claims the unexamined life leads to punishment after death
The greatest good is justice in the city; the unexamined life produces unjust citizens
The greatest good is daily conversation about virtue and wisdom; the life that is unexamined is not worth living

questions.feedback_correct: At Apology 38a, Socrates states: "The greatest good of man is daily to converse about virtue, and all that concerning which you hear me examining myself and others, and that the life which is unexamined is not worth living." This sentence is the philosophical program of the entire course in miniature: not that the philosopher is comfortable or successful, but that a life organized around honest inquiry engages what is genuinely important in a way that no other kind of life does.

quizzes.title: Week 2 Reading Quiz: Plato's Euthyphro
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Plato's Euthyphro.

questions.text: Where does the Euthyphro take place, and why is Socrates there?

answers.text: At Socrates' own trial, where the jury is deciding his sentence
At the court of the King Archon, where Socrates has come because Meletus has just filed the formal charge of impiety against him
In prison, where Socrates is awaiting execution after his conviction
At Euthyphro's family home, where his father is being formally sentenced

questions.feedback_correct: The Euthyphro is set before Socrates' trial, not after it. Socrates has come to the court of the King Archon (the official who handled religious and homicide cases) because Meletus is in the process of formally lodging the impiety charge against him. It is the Crito, a different dialogue, that is set later, during the wait between Socrates' conviction and his execution.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Euthyphro is set before Socrates' trial, not after it. Socrates has come to the court of the King Archon (the official who handled religious and homicide cases) because Meletus is in the process of formally lodging the impiety charge against him. It is the Crito, a different dialogue, that is set later, during the wait between Socrates' conviction and his execution.

questions.text: Why is Euthyphro at the court of the King Archon?

answers.text: He is prosecuting his own father for the death of a dependent laborer
He is defending himself against a charge of impiety
He is there to testify on Socrates' behalf
He is registering a property dispute with his family

questions.feedback_correct: Euthyphro tells Socrates he is bringing a charge against his own father. A dependent laborer had killed one of their household slaves; his father had the man bound and put aside while waiting for guidance from a religious expert. The man died before the messenger returned, and Euthyphro considers his father's negligence an act of impiety. The unconventional nature of a son prosecuting his own father is part of what makes the case philosophically interesting.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Euthyphro tells Socrates he is bringing a charge against his own father. A dependent laborer had killed one of their household slaves; his father had the man bound and put aside while waiting for guidance from a religious expert. The man died before the messenger returned, and Euthyphro considers his father's negligence an act of impiety. The unconventional nature of a son prosecuting his own father is part of what makes the case philosophically interesting.

questions.text: When Socrates first asks Euthyphro "What is piety?", Euthyphro's initial response is to:

answers.text: Admit that piety is too difficult to define and defer to the priests
Give the definition: piety is what is pleasing to all the gods
Argue that piety is the same as justice in all circumstances
Offer his own conduct, prosecuting his father, as an example of what piety is

questions.feedback_correct: Euthyphro's first answer is to point to what he is doing right now. Socrates rejects this immediately: he did not ask for an example but for the single Form that makes all pious acts pious. A list of pious actions cannot serve as a definition because it does not identify the principle that explains what makes them pious.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Euthyphro's first answer is to point to what he is doing right now. Socrates rejects this immediately: he did not ask for an example but for the single Form that makes all pious acts pious. A list of pious actions cannot serve as a definition because it does not identify the principle that explains what makes them pious.

questions.text: Socrates refutes Euthyphro's second definition, that piety is what is dear to the gods, by pointing out that:

answers.text: The gods do not actually exist and therefore cannot love anything
Because the gods quarrel and disagree, the same action could be both dear and hateful to the gods simultaneously, making the definition contradictory
Euthyphro himself does not believe in the traditional stories about the gods
What is dear to the gods changes over time and so cannot serve as a stable definition

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates gets Euthyphro to agree that the gods dispute about matters of justice and injustice. If different gods love and hate the same things, then the same action is both god-loved and god-hated. On Euthyphro's definition, it would therefore be both pious and impious at once, a contradiction that destroys the definition.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Socrates gets Euthyphro to agree that the gods dispute about matters of justice and injustice. If different gods love and hate the same things, then the same action is both god-loved and god-hated. On Euthyphro's definition, it would therefore be both pious and impious at once, a contradiction that destroys the definition.

questions.text: At the heart of the dialogue, Socrates poses the question that has since been called the "Euthyphro Dilemma." Which of the following best states the dilemma?

answers.text: Either the gods exist, in which case piety is possible, or they do not, in which case piety is meaningless
Either piety can be defined in terms of justice, or justice can be defined in terms of piety, but not both
Either the pious is loved by the gods because it is pious, or it is pious because it is loved by the gods, and Euthyphro's definition collapses on either horn
Either Euthyphro truly knows what piety is, or Socrates does, but the dialogue shows that neither does

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates argues that "god-loved" and "pious" cannot mean the same thing. If the gods love pious things because those things are already pious, then divine love is a response to piety, not a definition of it. If things are pious simply because the gods love them, then piety is arbitrary, a quality produced by divine preference rather than any nature of its own. Either way, Euthyphro's third definition fails.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Socrates argues that "god-loved" and "pious" cannot mean the same thing. If the gods love pious things because those things are already pious, then divine love is a response to piety, not a definition of it. If things are pious simply because the gods love them, then piety is arbitrary, a quality produced by divine preference rather than any nature of its own. Either way, Euthyphro's third definition fails.

questions.text: How does the dialogue end?

answers.text: Euthyphro arrives at a final, satisfactory definition of piety that Socrates accepts
Socrates concludes that piety is identical to justice
Euthyphro says he has discovered that piety cannot be taught, only felt
Euthyphro claims he is in a hurry and leaves; Socrates is no closer to knowing what piety is

questions.feedback_correct: The dialogue ends in aporia. After several definitions have been proposed and refuted, and after the conversation has circled back toward its starting point, Euthyphro says he must go and departs. Socrates remarks, with characteristic irony, that he had hoped to learn from Euthyphro what piety is so that he might use the knowledge in his own defense against the charge of impiety, but he is left without the answer he sought.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The dialogue ends in aporia. After several definitions have been proposed and refuted, and after the conversation has circled back toward its starting point, Euthyphro says he must go and departs. Socrates remarks, with characteristic irony, that he had hoped to learn from Euthyphro what piety is so that he might use the knowledge in his own defense against the charge of impiety, but he is left without the answer he sought.

quizzes.title: Week 3 Reading Quiz: Plato's Meno (70a-80d)
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Plato's Meno, 70a-80d.

questions.text: When Socrates asks Meno "What is virtue?", Meno's first response is to:

answers.text: List separate virtues for men, women, children, and slaves
Admit that he has no idea and ask Socrates to define it for him
Give a single universal definition: virtue is the power of governing
Argue that virtue cannot be defined at all, only practiced

questions.feedback_correct: Meno's opening move is to give examples rather than a definition: the virtue of a man is to manage the city well, a woman's virtue is to manage the household, and there are virtues for children, slaves, and free men. Socrates rejects this immediately: a list of examples does not identify the single nature that makes all of them virtues. The same objection applies here that applied to Euthyphro's first answer about piety.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Meno's opening move is to give examples rather than a definition: the virtue of a man is to manage the city well, a woman's virtue is to manage the household, and there are virtues for children, slaves, and free men. Socrates rejects this immediately: a list of examples does not identify the single nature that makes all of them virtues. The same objection applies here that applied to Euthyphro's first answer about piety.

questions.text: Socrates uses the image of a swarm of bees to make which point?

answers.text: That virtues are hard to catch and pin down
That bees and virtuous people both serve their communities
That the Sophists swarm around money the way bees swarm around flowers
That however many kinds of bees there are, they share a single common nature, and the same must be true of virtue

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates asks: if you were asked what a bee is, would you give a list of different kinds of bees? No; you would say what all bees share as bees. Virtue is the same: whatever the many virtues are, they must have a common nature that makes them all virtues. That common nature is what Socrates wants.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Socrates asks: if you were asked what a bee is, would you give a list of different kinds of bees? No; you would say what all bees share as bees. Virtue is the same: whatever the many virtues are, they must have a common nature that makes them all virtues. That common nature is what Socrates wants.

questions.text: Meno eventually compares Socrates to a torpedo fish (a numbing ray). What does this comparison mean in context?

answers.text: That Socrates is dangerous to the city and should be avoided
That Socrates is slow and methodical, like a creature lurking on the seafloor
That Socrates leaves those he questions unable to say what they thought they knew
That Socrates hides his real knowledge, the way a torpedo fish hides in the sand

questions.feedback_correct: Meno has given confident speeches about virtue many times before, but after a conversation with Socrates he finds himself unable even to say what virtue is. He compares this to the numbing shock of the torpedo fish. Socrates accepts the image but adds a qualification: he is equally at a loss himself, numbing others only because he is genuinely perplexed, not because he is cleverly concealing the answer.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Meno has given confident speeches about virtue many times before, but after a conversation with Socrates he finds himself unable even to say what virtue is. He compares this to the numbing shock of the torpedo fish. Socrates accepts the image but adds a qualification: he is equally at a loss himself, numbing others only because he is genuinely perplexed, not because he is cleverly concealing the answer.

questions.text: Meno raises what has come to be called "Meno's Paradox." Which of the following best states the paradox?

answers.text: If you already know what virtue is, you do not need to inquire; if you do not know at all, you cannot even recognize it when you find it, so inquiry seems impossible either way
Virtue cannot be defined because every person's experience of virtue is different
The Sophists teach virtue for money, but what they teach is not virtue, so genuine virtue cannot be taught
Since we cannot define virtue in words, the only way to know it is to act virtuously and observe the result

questions.feedback_correct: Meno's Paradox is a genuine epistemological puzzle: inquiry requires that you not already have the answer (otherwise it isn't inquiry), but it also requires that you be able to recognize the answer when you find it (otherwise you could never know you had succeeded). Complete ignorance makes recognition impossible; complete knowledge makes searching unnecessary. Both horns of the dilemma seem to rule out genuine inquiry.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Meno's Paradox is a genuine epistemological puzzle: inquiry requires that you not already have the answer (otherwise it isn't inquiry), but it also requires that you be able to recognize the answer when you find it (otherwise you could never know you had succeeded). Complete ignorance makes recognition impossible; complete knowledge makes searching unnecessary. Both horns of the dilemma seem to rule out genuine inquiry.

questions.text: Socrates' response to Meno's Paradox involves the doctrine of recollection (anamnesis). What does this doctrine claim?

answers.text: That the soul must experience many worldly pleasures before it can understand virtue
That all knowledge comes through the senses and must be built up through repeated experience
That wisdom is transmitted from teacher to student through dialogue, which is why Socrates calls himself a teacher despite his disclaimers
That the soul existed before birth, learned things in that prior existence, forgot them at birth, and recovers them through questioning, so "learning" is really recollecting

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates argues that the soul is immortal, that it has existed before this life and acquired knowledge, and that birth causes it to forget. What we call "learning" is actually re-acquiring, recollecting, knowledge that was already latent within us. This dissolves Meno's Paradox by identifying a state between complete knowledge and complete ignorance: dormant knowledge that can be recovered through the right kind of questioning.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Socrates argues that the soul is immortal, that it has existed before this life and acquired knowledge, and that birth causes it to forget. What we call "learning" is actually re-acquiring, recollecting, knowledge that was already latent within us. This dissolves Meno's Paradox by identifying a state between complete knowledge and complete ignorance: dormant knowledge that can be recovered through the right kind of questioning.

questions.text: In the slave boy demonstration, what is Socrates trying to show?

answers.text: That slaves can be educated to the same level as free citizens if treated with patience
That a person with no training in geometry can arrive at correct geometrical conclusions through questioning alone, suggesting the knowledge was already within him
That geometry is a universal language accessible to all people regardless of background
That Meno's slaves are better educated than Meno himself

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates questions one of Meno's slaves, who has received no mathematical education, and through questioning alone leads him to recognize the correct answer to a geometric problem about doubling the area of a square. The boy is not told the answer; he reasons his way to it. Socrates interprets this as evidence for recollection: the boy's knowledge was latent within him, and the questioning brought it to the surface.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Socrates questions one of Meno's slaves, who has received no mathematical education, and through questioning alone leads him to recognize the correct answer to a geometric problem about doubling the area of a square. The boy is not told the answer; he reasons his way to it. Socrates interprets this as evidence for recollection: the boy's knowledge was latent within him, and the questioning brought it to the surface.

quizzes.title: Week 4 Reading Quiz: Plato's Meno (80d-100b)
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Plato's Meno, 80d-100b.

questions.text: Socrates demonstrates the doctrine of recollection using Meno's slave boy. What does the demonstration show?

answers.text: That the boy, through questioning alone, reaches correct geometrical conclusions he was never taught, suggesting the knowledge was already within him
That a skilled teacher can implant knowledge in an untrained mind through careful instruction
That slaves are naturally more perceptive than their masters
That geometry is easier to learn than virtue because geometry has clear right answers

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates questions one of Meno's slave boys, who has received no mathematical education, and without providing any information, only questions, draws out the correct answer to a problem about doubling the area of a square. The demonstration is intended to show that the knowledge was latent within the boy, not supplied from outside. This is Socrates' answer to Meno's Paradox: we are not starting from complete ignorance, because knowledge is already within us in a dormant form.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Socrates questions one of Meno's slave boys, who has received no mathematical education, and without providing any information, only questions, draws out the correct answer to a problem about doubling the area of a square. The demonstration is intended to show that the knowledge was latent within the boy, not supplied from outside. This is Socrates' answer to Meno's Paradox: we are not starting from complete ignorance, because knowledge is already within us in a dormant form.

questions.text: What is the key difference Socrates draws between knowledge (episteme) and true opinion (doxa)?

answers.text: That knowledge is about mathematics and science; true opinion is about ethics and politics
That knowledge is always correct; true opinion may be correct or incorrect depending on luck
That knowledge comes from the gods; true opinion comes from human reasoning

That knowledge is a true belief with an account, tied down by understanding of the reason why, while true opinion is a true belief that lacks this grounding and therefore cannot be reliably transmitted or maintained

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates uses the image of the statues of Daedalus: true opinions are like those statues, beautiful and useful, but prone to "running away" because they are not fastened down. Knowledge, by contrast, is true belief tethered by an account of why it is true. This makes knowledge stable, transmissible, and reliable under new conditions in a way that true opinion is not.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Socrates uses the image of the statues of Daedalus: true opinions are like those statues, beautiful and useful, but prone to "running away" because they are not fastened down. Knowledge, by contrast, is true belief tethered by an account of why it is true. This makes knowledge stable, transmissible, and reliable under new conditions in a way that true opinion is not.

questions.text: Socrates uses the example of the road to Larissa to illustrate the knowledge/true opinion distinction. What is his point?

answers.text: That someone who has never traveled to Larissa cannot give correct directions to someone who is going there
That someone with merely true opinion and someone with genuine knowledge can both guide you correctly in familiar circumstances, but only the knower will reliably succeed when conditions change
That knowledge of geography is more reliable than knowledge of ethics, since geography can be checked empirically
That the Sophists are like false guides who claim to know the road to Larissa but are actually leading travelers astray

questions.feedback_correct: Both a person who has correct opinion about the road and a person who has traveled it themselves can give you the right directions to Larissa, both get you to the right destination. The difference emerges when circumstances change or when you need to explain the route to someone else. The knower understands why the road goes where it does; the person with true opinion merely happens to have the right belief.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Both a person who has correct opinion about the road and a person who has traveled it themselves can give you the right directions to Larissa, both get you to the right destination. The difference emerges when circumstances change or when you need to explain the route to someone else. The knower understands why the road goes where it does; the person with true opinion merely happens to have the right belief.

questions.text: Socrates argues that virtue cannot be taught by examining which piece of evidence about great Athenian statesmen?

answers.text: That the greatest Athenian statesmen all denied being virtuous
That the Sophists, despite charging high fees, never produced students who became statesmen
That famous virtuous statesmen like Pericles and Themistocles consistently failed to produce virtuous sons, despite having every opportunity and motivation to do so
That Athenian democracy produced fewer virtuous leaders than Spartan oligarchy

questions.feedback_correct: If virtue were a form of transmissible knowledge, one would expect the most virtuous men to be able to teach it, especially to their own sons, under optimal conditions. But Pericles' sons were undistinguished. Themistocles' sons were known for equestrian accomplishments, not virtue. This consistent failure to transmit virtue through even the most favorable channels suggests that virtue is not taught the way a craft or a science is taught.
questions.feedback_incorrect: If virtue were a form of transmissible knowledge, one would expect the most virtuous men to be able to teach it, especially to their own sons, under optimal conditions. But Pericles' sons were undistinguished. Themistocles' sons were known for equestrian accomplishments, not virtue. This consistent failure to transmit virtue through even the most favorable channels suggests that virtue is not taught the way a craft or a science is taught.

questions.text: At the end of the dialogue, Socrates concludes that virtue in successful statesmen is best explained as:

answers.text: A kind of divine gift or right opinion, not grounded in genuine knowledge, like the inspired speech of poets and prophets
Knowledge that is so deep it cannot be articulated
A natural talent, like athletic ability, that some people are born with
The result of rigorous training by the Sophists

questions.feedback_correct: Since no reliable teachers of virtue can be found, virtue cannot be knowledge in the full sense (which would make it teachable). Since good men consistently fail to produce virtuous sons, it is not a natural endowment either. Socrates concludes that the virtuous succeed by a kind of divine inspiration, true opinion granted as a gift, not secured by reasoned understanding. He compares them to inspired poets who say true things without knowing what they mean.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Since no reliable teachers of virtue can be found, virtue cannot be knowledge in the full sense (which would make it teachable). Since good men consistently fail to produce virtuous sons, it is not a natural endowment either. Socrates concludes that the virtuous succeed by a kind of divine inspiration, true opinion granted as a gift, not secured by reasoned understanding. He compares them to inspired poets who say true things without knowing what they mean.

questions.text: Socrates says the Meno's conclusion about virtue is provisional. Why is it provisional, and what does he say is needed before a more confident answer can be given?

answers.text: Because more historical research needs to be done on Athenian statesmen before we can be certain
Because the answer depends on whether the gods actually exist, which has not been established in this dialogue
Because the slave boy demonstration needs to be repeated with more subjects before it is philosophically conclusive
Because we cannot settle whether virtue is teachable until we first know what virtue is, and the earlier inquiry into what virtue is remained unresolved

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates says explicitly near the end of the dialogue that the question of how virtue comes to us cannot be settled until the prior question, what virtue itself is, has been answered. The Meno attempted to define virtue and failed. That failure means the conclusion about teachability rests on an incomplete foundation. The investigation into what virtue is remains open, which is why the Meno ends not with a settled answer but with an honest acknowledgment that the harder inquiry has not yet been done.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Socrates says explicitly near the end of the dialogue that the question of how virtue comes to us cannot be settled until the prior question, what virtue itself is, has been answered. The Meno attempted to define virtue and failed. That failure means the conclusion about teachability rests on an incomplete foundation. The investigation into what virtue is remains open, which is why the Meno ends not with a settled answer but with an honest acknowledgment that the harder inquiry has not yet been done.
