quizzes.title: Week 5 Reading Quiz: Aquinas and Paley
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Aquinas's Summa Theologica I q.2 a.1-3 and Paley's Natural Theology ch. 1.

questions.text: In his Summa Theologica, Aquinas presents two objections to God's existence before giving his own arguments for it. What is the purpose of this structure?

answers.text: To show that the objections are easy to dismiss and should not be taken seriously
To comply with Church rules requiring that heretical arguments be acknowledged before being condemned
To persuade readers who already doubt God's existence by presenting their doubts in the most flattering light
To model rigorous philosophical method: a strong argument must engage the best objections against it, not ignore them

questions.feedback_correct: Aquinas's method, state the strongest objections first, then reply to them at the end, reflects the standard of intellectual honesty he learned from Aristotle and from the practice of scholastic disputation. A position is only as strong as its engagement with the best arguments against it. This method is exactly what the Aquinas essay assignment asks you to practice: represent the opposing argument fairly before you challenge or defend it.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Aquinas's method, state the strongest objections first, then reply to them at the end, reflects the standard of intellectual honesty he learned from Aristotle and from the practice of scholastic disputation. A position is only as strong as its engagement with the best arguments against it. This method is exactly what the Aquinas essay assignment asks you to practice: represent the opposing argument fairly before you challenge or defend it.

questions.text: In the First Way, Aquinas argues from the existence of motion to a first unmoved mover. What is his reason for claiming that a chain of movers cannot extend back infinitely?

answers.text: If the chain of movers had no first member, there would be no source of motion at all, and therefore nothing would be moving, yet motion clearly exists
Infinite chains are logically contradictory because infinity cannot be a real quantity
The Church teaches that the universe had a definite beginning, so an eternal chain of movers is theologically ruled out
Aristotle had already proved that the number of movers must be finite, and Aquinas accepts Aristotle's authority on this point

questions.feedback_correct: Aquinas's argument is that subsequent movers only move because they are moved by something prior. If there is no first mover, nothing that moves without itself being moved, then the chain as a whole has no source of motion, and motion becomes impossible. But we see motion. Therefore there must be a first mover. Note: Aquinas is not making the theological claim that the universe had a beginning in time; that is a separate question he treats elsewhere.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Aquinas's argument is that subsequent movers only move because they are moved by something prior. If there is no first mover, nothing that moves without itself being moved, then the chain as a whole has no source of motion, and motion becomes impossible. But we see motion. Therefore there must be a first mover. Note: Aquinas is not making the theological claim that the universe had a beginning in time; that is a separate question he treats elsewhere.

questions.text: The Third Way argues from contingency to a necessary being. What does Aquinas mean when he says that if everything were contingent, "there would have been nothing in existence"?

answers.text: Contingent things are illusory; only necessary things truly exist, so a world of purely contingent things would be a world of illusions
Contingency means uncertainty, and a world of purely uncertain things would collapse into chaos and cease to function
If every individual thing is mortal or temporary, then at some point all things might simultaneously cease to exist, and once there is nothing, nothing can come from nothing
God created the world at the beginning of time, and without that original creation there would have been nothing, which proves creation must have occurred

questions.feedback_correct: A contingent thing is one that can exist or fail to exist. If every thing in existence has this character, if nothing exists by necessity, then there is a possible state of affairs in which nothing exists at all. But if there were ever genuinely nothing, nothing could emerge from it, because nothing produces nothing. The fact that something exists now requires that there be something that exists necessarily, which cannot not exist.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A contingent thing is one that can exist or fail to exist. If every thing in existence has this character, if nothing exists by necessity, then there is a possible state of affairs in which nothing exists at all. But if there were ever genuinely nothing, nothing could emerge from it, because nothing produces nothing. The fact that something exists now requires that there be something that exists necessarily, which cannot not exist.

questions.text: In the opening of Natural Theology, Paley distinguishes between finding a stone and finding a watch on a heath. What is the precise feature of the watch that makes it different from the stone and forces the inference to a designer?

answers.text: The watch is made of metal, which does not occur naturally, so it must have been manufactured
The watch's parts are fitted together in a specific way that serves a definite purpose, telling time, and this purposive organization cannot be explained without invoking intention
The watch is much more complex than the stone, and complexity is always evidence of intelligent design
The watch is fragile and could not have survived natural processes, so it must have been placed there recently by a human being

questions.feedback_correct: Paley's key distinction is not size, material, or complexity alone, but purposive organization: the parts of the watch are arranged precisely to produce a specific result. A stone's parts are not arranged to serve any purpose. This fitness of parts to an end is, for Paley, the mark of design, and the mark he then finds throughout the natural world.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Paley's key distinction is not size, material, or complexity alone, but purposive organization: the parts of the watch are arranged precisely to produce a specific result. A stone's parts are not arranged to serve any purpose. This fitness of parts to an end is, for Paley, the mark of design, and the mark he then finds throughout the natural world.

questions.text: Paley considers the objection that a defective or imperfect watch would not compel the inference to a designer. How does he reply?

answers.text: He concedes the point: a badly made watch does raise doubt about whether any designer existed
He rejects the objection by arguing that nature is never imperfect; apparent imperfections are always shown by science to serve hidden purposes
He agrees that imperfection raises a problem for the analogy, which is why he bases his main argument on the eye rather than the watch
A defective watch is evidence of a careless or incompetent designer, not of no designer at all; the purposive structure remains visible even when the execution is imperfect

questions.feedback_correct: Paley's point is that imperfection does not erase the evidence of design; it qualifies it. A broken watch still has the structure of a designed object, springs, gears, a dial, even if it is not functioning well. Similarly, the fact that organisms sometimes fail or suffer from disease does not undermine the inference to design; at most it raises questions about the quality or purposes of the designer.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Paley's point is that imperfection does not erase the evidence of design; it qualifies it. A broken watch still has the structure of a designed object, springs, gears, a dial, even if it is not functioning well. Similarly, the fact that organisms sometimes fail or suffer from disease does not undermine the inference to design; at most it raises questions about the quality or purposes of the designer.

questions.text: Paley applies the watchmaker analogy to the human eye. What is the philosophical move he is making, and what risk does that move carry?

answers.text: He is making an argument from analogy: the eye resembles a watch in the relevant respects, so what explains the watch (a designer) explains the eye too. The risk is that if the two things differ in ways that matter, the analogy fails.
He is making an inductive argument: because some natural things (eyes) appear designed, probably all natural things are designed. The risk is that induction is never certain.
He is making a deductive argument from the definition of "design": anything with functioning parts is by definition designed. The risk is that this definition may be question-begging.

He is making a statistical argument: the probability that the eye arose by chance is so low that design is the only reasonable alternative. The risk is that probability estimates about unique events are unreliable.

questions.feedback_correct: Paley's argument is fundamentally analogical. Because the eye, like the watch, has parts fitted together to serve a definite purpose (seeing), and because purposive organization in the watch requires a watchmaker, purposive organization in the eye requires a designer too. The risk is that the analogy may not hold: the eye differs from the watch in significant ways, it is organic, it developed from a single cell, it replicates, and those differences may break the analogy. This is exactly the pressure point Hume exploits in the Dialogues, and it is the background against which Darwin's theory of natural selection became so philosophically significant.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Paley's argument is fundamentally analogical. Because the eye, like the watch, has parts fitted together to serve a definite purpose (seeing), and because purposive organization in the watch requires a watchmaker, purposive organization in the eye requires a designer too. The risk is that the analogy may not hold: the eye differs from the watch in significant ways, it is organic, it developed from a single cell, it replicates, and those differences may break the analogy. This is exactly the pressure point Hume exploits in the Dialogues, and it is the background against which Darwin's theory of natural selection became so philosophically significant.

quizzes.title: Week 6 Reading Quiz: Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Hume's Dialogues Concerning Natural Religion, Parts I-IV.

questions.text: Hume's Dialogues presents three main characters in debate. Which of the following correctly identifies each character's position?

answers.text: Cleanthes defends the Design Argument from empirical analogy; Philo is the philosophical skeptic; Demea is the orthodox rationalist who emphasizes God's incomprehensibility
Cleanthes defends the impossibility of natural theology; Philo argues from scripture; Demea defends the Design Argument
Cleanthes is the atheist; Philo defends religion through faith; Demea defends religion through reason
All three characters agree that God exists but disagree only about how to describe God's nature

questions.feedback_correct: Cleanthes is the empirical theist: he argues that the order of nature, like the mechanism of a machine, supports the inference to an intelligent Creator. Philo applies skeptical pressure to that argument throughout the dialogue, questioning whether the analogy between nature and human artifacts can bear the weight Cleanthes places on it. Demea accepts God's existence but believes reason leads to a God whose nature transcends human comprehension, quite different from Cleanthes' human-like designer.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Cleanthes is the empirical theist: he argues that the order of nature, like the mechanism of a machine, supports the inference to an intelligent Creator. Philo applies skeptical pressure to that argument throughout the dialogue, questioning whether the analogy between nature and human artifacts can bear the weight Cleanthes places on it. Demea accepts God's existence but believes reason leads to a God whose nature transcends human comprehension, quite different from Cleanthes' human-like designer.

questions.text: Philo's most fundamental objection in Part II is about the limits of analogy when applied to the universe. What is that objection?

answers.text: The universe does not actually display purposive order, it only appears to do so because we are conditioned by language to see purpose everywhere
The Design Argument is valid only if God is already assumed to exist, which makes it circular
Analogical reasoning is never legitimate in philosophy and should always be replaced with deductive proof
We have experience of only one universe and have never observed another universe being made, so we cannot draw reliable analogical inferences about what kind of process produces universes

questions.feedback_correct: The force of an analogical inference depends on the breadth and quality of the experience behind it. We can infer watchmakers from watches because we have extensive experience of how watches come to be. We have no comparable experience of universe-making. We have observed exactly one universe and have no knowledge of its origin. Philo's point is that extending the analogical inference to a conclusion about the universe's cause goes far beyond what our experience licenses.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The force of an analogical inference depends on the breadth and quality of the experience behind it. We can infer watchmakers from watches because we have extensive experience of how watches come to be. We have no comparable experience of universe-making. We have observed exactly one universe and have no knowledge of its origin. Philo's point is that extending the analogical inference to a conclusion about the universe's cause goes far beyond what our experience licenses.

questions.text: Cleanthes argues in Part III that Philo is setting an unreasonably high standard for the Design Argument. What is Cleanthes' defense?

answers.text: The Design Argument is a deductive proof, not an analogy, so Philo's objections are irrelevant
Philo has privately admitted to Cleanthes that the argument is valid; his public skepticism is merely a rhetorical pose

We regularly accept causal inferences based on single cases when the evidence is sufficiently striking, and the order of the universe is compelling enough to support an inference even without a wide sample
The authority of scripture supplements the Design Argument and fills in whatever gaps reason cannot close

questions.feedback_correct: Cleanthes argues that analogical inferences need not await a large sample of comparable cases to be credible. We infer causes from single effects all the time, from a document, from a fossil, from the ruins of a building, without observing a range of similar cases being produced. The order of the universe is sufficiently striking and sufficiently similar to designed order that the inference, while not certain, is reasonable. This is the core of Cleanthes' defense against Philo's skeptical pressure.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Cleanthes argues that analogical inferences need not await a large sample of comparable cases to be credible. We infer causes from single effects all the time, from a document, from a fossil, from the ruins of a building, without observing a range of similar cases being produced. The order of the universe is sufficiently striking and sufficiently similar to designed order that the inference, while not certain, is reasonable. This is the core of Cleanthes' defense against Philo's skeptical pressure.

questions.text: Philo points out in Part II that, if the analogy between the universe and a human artifact is taken seriously, it might equally support polytheism as monotheism. What is his reasoning?

answers.text: All the large and complex objects we know of, ships, cities, cathedrals, are typically the products of many minds collaborating, so if the universe resembles a large artifact, it resembles the products of a team more than the product of a single mind
Since the universe is so large, only a committee of gods could have made it; no single mind is capable of conceiving something so vast
Ancient peoples were polytheists who built the most impressive artifacts in history, which shows that great design often comes from many minds working together
The three characters in the Dialogues each represent a different god, and the fact that they disagree suggests that no single god controls the universe

questions.feedback_correct: Philo's argument is that the analogy, pressed consistently, undermines the monotheistic conclusion rather than supporting it. The grandest human artifacts are team projects, not the work of solitary designers. If we infer a designer from the scale and complexity of the universe, the analogy gives us more reason to expect a committee of designers than a single one. Cleanthes cannot selectively apply the analogy to get the parts of it he wants while ignoring the parts that complicate his conclusion.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Philo's argument is that the analogy, pressed consistently, undermines the monotheistic conclusion rather than supporting it. The grandest human artifacts are team projects, not the work of solitary designers. If we infer a designer from the scale and complexity of the universe, the analogy gives us more reason to expect a committee of designers than a single one. Cleanthes cannot selectively apply the analogy to get the parts of it he wants while ignoring the parts that complicate his conclusion.

questions.text: In Part IV, Demea objects that Cleanthes' argument leads to an unacceptably "anthropomorphic" God. What does this objection mean, and why does Demea consider it a theological problem?

answers.text: Anthropomorphism means giving God a human body, which Cleanthes' argument does, since the argument is based on a human artifact
Demea objects because Cleanthes uses the wrong translation of the Bible, and the correct translation does not support the Design Argument
Anthropomorphism means projecting human emotions onto God, and Demea objects because an emotional God would be unstable and unreliable

Demea believes that God is infinite and incomprehensible, radically unlike any creature, and that Cleanthes' argument, by comparing God's mind to a human mind, reduces God to a superior version of a creature rather than a being of a fundamentally different kind

questions.feedback_correct: "Anthropomorphism" means attributing human characteristics to God. Cleanthes concludes that the Author of Nature has "a mind similar to the human mind." Demea finds this theologically unacceptable: the God of orthodox theology is not a large version of a human mind. God is infinite, eternal, simple, and utterly unlike anything in creation. By modeling God on the human designer, Cleanthes has, in Demea's view, made God a creature, one far more powerful than us, but still of the same fundamental kind. This is a reduction, not an elevation.
questions.feedback_incorrect: "Anthropomorphism" means attributing human characteristics to God. Cleanthes concludes that the Author of Nature has "a mind similar to the human mind." Demea finds this theologically unacceptable: the God of orthodox theology is not a large version of a human mind. God is infinite, eternal, simple, and utterly unlike anything in creation. By modeling God on the human designer, Cleanthes has, in Demea's view, made God a creature, one far more powerful than us, but still of the same fundamental kind. This is a reduction, not an elevation.

questions.text: In Part IV, Philo presses a "regress of mind" argument against Cleanthes. What is that argument, and what does it reveal about the Design Argument's structure?

answers.text: Philo argues that God must have a brain in order to think, and a brain is a physical object that requires a physical cause, leading to an infinite regress of physical causes

Philo argues that if organized complexity always requires an intelligent cause, then God's own intelligent mind, which is supremely organized, requires an intelligent cause too; this either produces an infinite regress or shows that the principle "order requires a mind" cannot be the stopping point the argument needs
Philo argues that the regress of efficient causes Aquinas described in the Second Way applies equally to God, and therefore Aquinas's argument for God's existence contradicts Cleanthes' argument
Philo shows that Cleanthes' argument requires an actual infinite regress of past causes, which he proves is impossible, and therefore the argument collapses

questions.feedback_correct: The force of Philo's argument is to turn Cleanthes' own principle back on itself. Cleanthes says: wherever we find order, we should infer a mind that produced it. But a divine mind is maximally ordered, presumably the most organized thing in existence. By Cleanthes' principle, God's mind requires a cause. Either there is an infinite regress of ordering minds, or some ordering mind is self-explanatory. But if some mind can be self-explanatory, if some ordered thing needs no further cause, then why cannot matter be self-explanatory? The argument seems to need a stopping point that it cannot provide on its own terms.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The force of Philo's argument is to turn Cleanthes' own principle back on itself. Cleanthes says: wherever we find order, we should infer a mind that produced it. But a divine mind is maximally ordered, presumably the most organized thing in existence. By Cleanthes' principle, God's mind requires a cause. Either there is an infinite regress of ordering minds, or some ordering mind is self-explanatory. But if some mind can be self-explanatory, if some ordered thing needs no further cause, then why cannot matter be self-explanatory? The argument seems to need a stopping point that it cannot provide on its own terms.

quizzes.title: Week 7 Reading Quiz: Lewis, Mere Christianity Book I
quizzes.description: 4 questions on C. S. Lewis, Mere Christianity, Book I, chs. 1-4.

questions.text: Lewis opens Mere Christianity with the observation that human beings quarrel. What philosophical point does he draw from the way people actually argue with each other?

answers.text: That human beings are naturally selfish, which is why they fight over resources and status
That quarreling is evidence of a fallen human nature, and philosophy cannot improve on what religion has already diagnosed
That social conventions like "I was there first" are arbitrary rules that different cultures create differently, with no common foundation

That when people quarrel, they appeal to a standard, a principle of fairness or right conduct, that they expect the other party to recognize as binding on both of them, which shows they believe in an objective moral standard

questions.feedback_correct: Lewis's point is not about the content of quarrels but about their form. When someone says "That's not fair" or "You promised," they are not merely expressing a preference; they are invoking a standard they expect their opponent to recognize. Both parties argue within a shared framework of moral expectations, treating the other person as bound by the same rules. This is Lewis's evidence that a real Moral Law exists, one that is not merely personal or conventional.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Lewis's point is not about the content of quarrels but about their form. When someone says "That's not fair" or "You promised," they are not merely expressing a preference; they are invoking a standard they expect their opponent to recognize. Both parties argue within a shared framework of moral expectations, treating the other person as bound by the same rules. This is Lewis's evidence that a real Moral Law exists, one that is not merely personal or conventional.

questions.text: Lewis argues that the Moral Law is not the same as instinct. Which of the following best captures his reason?

answers.text: We frequently experience conflicting instincts, and something, the Moral Law, adjudicates between them by telling us which instinct we ought to follow; that adjudicating standard cannot itself be just another instinct
Instinct is an animal characteristic; morality is uniquely human because of our capacity for language
Instincts are always selfish, but morality often requires us to act against our own interests
Instinct is determined by genetics, but morality is entirely learned from culture and has no biological basis

questions.feedback_correct: Lewis's argument is structural: the Moral Law operates at a different level than instinct. When we feel both the pull of self-preservation and the pull to help someone in danger, something in us evaluates which pull we should follow. That evaluating standard, whatever tells us "in this case, you should help even though it costs you," cannot itself be reduced to one of the instincts being evaluated. It is meta-level, and that meta-level is what Lewis means by the Moral Law.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Lewis's argument is structural: the Moral Law operates at a different level than instinct. When we feel both the pull of self-preservation and the pull to help someone in danger, something in us evaluates which pull we should follow. That evaluating standard, whatever tells us "in this case, you should help even though it costs you," cannot itself be reduced to one of the instincts being evaluated. It is meta-level, and that meta-level is what Lewis means by the Moral Law.

questions.text: Lewis distinguishes two "views of the universe" in Book I, Chapter 4. Which of the following correctly identifies both views and their significance for his argument?

answers.text: The ancient view (the universe is eternal and uncreated) versus the modern view (the universe had a beginning in time); Lewis argues that cosmology proves there must be a Creator
The optimistic view (evil is outweighed by good) versus the pessimistic view (evil outweighs good); Lewis uses the balance of evidence to show that the world was designed for good

The materialist view (the universe is purposeless matter governed by physical laws) versus the religious view (something with the character of a mind is behind the universe); the Moral Law, Lewis argues, better fits the second view than the first
The Eastern view (God is impersonal energy) versus the Western view (God is a person); Lewis argues that the Moral Law requires a personal God specifically

questions.feedback_correct: The key contrast Lewis draws is between a universe that simply is, purposeless matter, no mind behind it, no standards embedded in it, and a universe that came from something with the character of mind and intention. The Moral Law is Lewis's evidence for preferring the second view: a purely material universe has no place for a real "ought," but the "ought" that the Moral Law embodies is unmistakably real.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The key contrast Lewis draws is between a universe that simply is, purposeless matter, no mind behind it, no standards embedded in it, and a universe that came from something with the character of mind and intention. The Moral Law is Lewis's evidence for preferring the second view: a purely material universe has no place for a real "ought," but the "ought" that the Moral Law embodies is unmistakably real.

questions.text: What is the core logical move of Lewis's Moral Argument for the existence of God?

answers.text: The existence of a real, objective Moral Law, one not produced by any human being or institution, implies the existence of a non-human moral lawgiver, which must be something like a mind concerned with right conduct
The universe is so complex that only God could have designed it, therefore God exists
Since evil exists and God is good, God must have created evil for some purpose; that purpose is the development of human virtue
The fact that all human cultures believe in some God proves that God must exist, since universal beliefs track reality

questions.feedback_correct: Lewis's argument is from moral law to moral lawgiver. If there is a standard of right and wrong that applies to all human beings, was not made by any human being or institution, and can be used to judge human institutions themselves, then something beyond the human made it. Whatever sets an objective moral standard for all rational beings must be something like a mind, something with intelligence, intention, and concern for conduct. This is what the tradition calls God.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Lewis's argument is from moral law to moral lawgiver. If there is a standard of right and wrong that applies to all human beings, was not made by any human being or institution, and can be used to judge human institutions themselves, then something beyond the human made it. Whatever sets an objective moral standard for all rational beings must be something like a mind, something with intelligence, intention, and concern for conduct. This is what the tradition calls God.

quizzes.title: Week 8 Reading Quiz: The Problem of Evil
quizzes.description: 6 questions on the Problem of Evil (Hume, Dialogues Part XI; Lewis, Mere Christianity Book I ch. 5).

questions.text: Which of the following correctly distinguishes the logical and evidential problems of evil?

answers.text: The logical problem claims God's existence and evil's existence are strictly incompatible; the evidential problem claims the amount and distribution of evil makes God's existence improbable without claiming strict contradiction
The logical problem is about natural evil; the evidential problem is about moral evil
The logical problem was invented by Hume; the evidential problem was invented by Epicurus
The logical problem can be solved by faith alone; the evidential problem requires scientific evidence

questions.feedback_correct: The logical problem is the stronger claim: that "God exists" and "evil exists" cannot both be true. Most contemporary philosophers think the Free Will Defense shows this version is not decisive. The evidential problem is more modest and more resilient: it does not require strict contradiction, only that the scale, distribution, and character of actual evil makes an omnipotent, omniscient, all-good God less probable.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The logical problem is the stronger claim: that "God exists" and "evil exists" cannot both be true. Most contemporary philosophers think the Free Will Defense shows this version is not decisive. The evidential problem is more modest and more resilient: it does not require strict contradiction, only that the scale, distribution, and character of actual evil makes an omnipotent, omniscient, all-good God less probable.

questions.text: Which of these is the clearest example of natural evil rather than moral evil?

answers.text: A CEO knowingly sells a defective product to increase profit
A government official accepts a bribe to overlook safety violations
A previously healthy child develops a fatal genetic disorder with no external cause
A soldier disobeys orders and assaults a prisoner of war

questions.feedback_correct: Moral evil results from the free choices of rational agents; options A, B, and D all involve someone's free decision to act wrongly. A genetic disorder with no external cause results from the natural order itself, not from anyone's choice, which is exactly what defines natural evil.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Moral evil results from the free choices of rational agents; options A, B, and D all involve someone's free decision to act wrongly. A genetic disorder with no external cause results from the natural order itself, not from anyone's choice, which is exactly what defines natural evil.

questions.text: What is the core claim of the Free Will Defense?

answers.text: God does not actually have the power to prevent moral evil, so God cannot be blamed for it
Evil is an illusion produced by limited human perspective on a fundamentally good universe
Human free will was corrupted at the Fall, so present-day moral evil is a punishment for original sin

Genuine freedom to choose between good and evil is a good of such high value that a world containing free beings who sometimes choose evil is better than a world of beings mechanically compelled to do good

questions.feedback_correct: The Free Will Defense holds that a world of genuinely free creatures capable of freely choosing the good is better than a world of beings who are compelled to do good, even though genuine freedom entails the real possibility of choosing evil. The suffering caused by human choices is the cost of that higher good, not evidence against a good God.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Free Will Defense holds that a world of genuinely free creatures capable of freely choosing the good is better than a world of beings who are compelled to do good, even though genuine freedom entails the real possibility of choosing evil. The suffering caused by human choices is the cost of that higher good, not evidence against a good God.

questions.text: What is the most serious objection to the Free Will Defense discussed in this week's lessons?

answers.text: It assumes human beings do not actually have free will, which contradicts its own premise
It does not address natural evil at all, since earthquakes, disease, and other forms of natural suffering are not produced by anyone's free choice
It proves too much, since it would justify literally any amount of moral evil no matter how severe
It was rejected by Aquinas, whose authority the course has already established as decisive

questions.feedback_correct: Whatever its force against moral evil, the Free Will Defense has nothing to say about suffering that has no human choice behind it: earthquakes, childhood cancer, predation. This gap is exactly why a separate response, the soul-making theodicy, was developed specifically to address natural evil.

quizzes.description: 6 questions on Plato's Phaedo, 57a-84b.

questions.text: According to Socrates in the Phaedo, what is death?

answers.text: The separation of the soul from the body
The annihilation of the person entirely
The permanent sleep of the mind
The return of matter to its original elements

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates defines death precisely at Phaedo 64c: it is the separation of the soul from the body. This definition is foundational to the entire argument of the dialogue. It does not mean the destruction of the person, but the departure of the person, the soul, from its temporary bodily home.

questions.text: Socrates argues that philosophers are "practicing dying and being dead" (64a). What does he mean?

Philosophy weakens the body by denying it physical pleasure
Philosophers have longer lifespans because they avoid physical excess
Philosophical practice separates the soul from the body by turning attention away from the senses toward pure thought

questions.feedback_correct: Socrates's point is that philosophy is a lifelong practice of doing what death accomplishes literally: withdrawing the soul from the body by directing the mind away from sensation and appetite toward abstract, rational inquiry. Opposites are always equal in magnitude
Everything that has a contrary comes from its contrary
Nature tends toward the stronger of any pair of opposites

questions.feedback_correct: The Cyclical Argument (69e-72e) rests on the observation that opposites generate each other in a continuous cycle: the large from the small, the sleeping from the waking, the living from the dead. This bidirectional process prevents any one opposite from consuming the other entirely. Socrates applies this to life and death to argue that the living must come from the dead, meaning souls must exist between lives.

Mathematical calculations involving large numbers
The names and histories of past events
Moral rules learned in childhood

Things we can know versus things we cannot know
Living things versus nonliving things
The visible, changing, never self-consistent versus the invisible, unchanging, always the same

quizzes.description: 6 questions on Descartes's Meditations on First Philosophy, Meditation VI.

questions.text: What is Descartes' cogito argument, and what does it establish?

answers.text: "I think, therefore I am": it establishes that the self exists, at minimum, as a thinking thing
"I feel, therefore I am": it establishes that the body is the seat of identity
"I doubt, therefore God exists": it establishes the existence of a divine guarantor of truth
"I perceive, therefore the external world exists": it establishes the reality of the physical world

questions.feedback_correct: The cogito ("cogito ergo sum") is Descartes' discovery in Meditation II that the one thing he cannot doubt is that he is doubting, and doubting is a form of thinking. Therefore he must exist, at minimum, as a thinking thing (res cogitans). This provides his indubitable foundation. The external world and the body require further argument to establish.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The cogito ("cogito ergo sum") is Descartes' discovery in Meditation II that the one thing he cannot doubt is that he is doubting, and doubting is a form of thinking. questions.text: In Meditation VI, Descartes argues for a "real distinction" between mind and body. What does he mean by this?

answers.text: The mind and body feel different, though they are the same substance
Mind and body are two separate aspects of a single unified substance
The distinction between mind and body is real only during life; at death they reunite
Mind and body are two completely different kinds of substance, each capable of existing without the other

questions.text: What is the "interaction problem" in Descartes' substance dualism?

The problem of explaining how a non-physical mind can causally affect a physical body, and vice versa
The problem of determining whether animals have souls
The problem of proving that God exists in order to guarantee the reliability of the senses

questions.text: How does functionalism differ from identity theory as an account of the mind?

answers.text: Identity theory says mental states are identical to specific brain states; functionalism says mental states are defined by their causal roles and can be multiply realized
Functionalism says mental states are identical to specific brain states; identity theory says they are defined by causal roles
Functionalism denies that mental states exist; identity theory affirms them
Identity theory is a form of dualism; functionalism is a form of eliminativism

questions.text: Philosopher David Chalmers distinguishes "easy problems" of consciousness from the "hard problem." What is the hard problem?

answers.text: Explaining how the brain integrates sensory information from different sources
Explaining why damage to specific brain regions produces specific behavioral deficits
Explaining why physical brain processes give rise to subjective experience, why there is something it is like to be conscious
Explaining how the brain distinguishes between sleep and waking states

That gap between physical process and subjective experience is what makes the mind-body problem genuinely hard.

quizzes.description: 6 questions on Plato's Phaedo 85b-118a and Republic IV.

questions.text: What is Simmias's Harmony Objection to the soul's immortality?

answers.text: The soul cannot survive without the body because it is made of the same matter
The soul might be the attunement of the body, an invisible but body-dependent property that ceases when the body is destroyed
Musical harmony proves the soul is eternal, since music outlasts individual performances
The soul is too complex to survive intact after death

questions.feedback_correct: Simmias argues at 85e-86d that the soul might be like the harmony of a well-tuned lyre: invisible, admirable, and real, but entirely dependent on the physical instrument for its existence. Destroy the lyre and the harmony ceases; destroy the body and the soul may cease just as completely, even though neither harmony nor soul is a visible physical thing.

questions.text: Socrates replies to Simmias in part by pointing out that the soul regularly opposes the body, for instance, in acts of self-control. Why does this refute the Harmony Objection?

answers.text: A harmony cannot oppose or overrule the very elements that constitute it, but the soul does exactly this to the body
It shows that the soul is physically stronger than the body
Self-control proves that the soul is made of a more durable material than the body
It shows the soul existed before the body, which a harmony cannot do

But Socrates argues that the soul regularly resists bodily impulses: it restrains hunger, masters fear, subdues desire. A thing that can overrule its substrate cannot be merely the harmony of that substrate.

But Socrates argues that the soul regularly resists bodily impulses: it restrains hunger, masters fear, subdues desire. A thing that can overrule its substrate cannot be merely the harmony of that substrate.

questions.text: What is the essential structure of Cebes's Cloak Objection?

answers.text: The soul, like a weaver's cloak, is woven together from physical threads and will unravel at death
Cloaks and souls share the same material, so the soul is mortal
The soul is a craftsman who builds bodies and then abandons them when they wear out
The soul may outlast many bodies, as a weaver outlasts many cloaks, but still eventually wear out and perish

questions.feedback_correct: Cebes argues at 87b-88b that even if the soul pre-existed this body and will survive into the next, this establishes persistence, not indestructibility. questions.text: In the Final Argument, Socrates introduces the concept of things that "always bring" a particular Form with them. What conclusion does this lead to about the soul?

answers.text: The soul is a Form, and Forms are indestructible by definition
The soul always brings knowledge with it, which is why the slave boy in the Meno could do geometry
The soul always brings life with it the way fire always brings heat, so the soul cannot admit death and is therefore deathless and imperishable
The soul, like fire, will eventually burn out and cease to exist

Socrates argues the soul is related to life the same way: whatever body it enters, it enters alive, and whatever body it departs, it departs dead. The complete suppression of appetite and spirit so that reason can operate alone
Following the laws of one's city, since the laws are themselves an expression of reason
Feeling no internal conflict at all, since a fully virtuous soul has only rational desires

That reason is supposed to govern the other parts or faculties of the self

That the body is entirely irrelevant to understanding the soul

Socrates's lifelong habitation in Athens, which constitutes an implicit agreement to abide by its legal processes
The religious duty to respect institutions established by the gods

questions.text: In the Ring of Gyges thought experiment, Glaucon argues that a person who possessed the ring would act unjustly without hesitation. What philosophical conclusion is he trying to establish?

answers.text: Justice is observed only because people fear punishment, not because it is genuinely valued for itself
Invisibility would corrupt even a virtuous person by exposing them to temptation they cannot resist
The gods punish invisible injustice even when human law cannot
Power corrupts: the more control a person has, the more likely they are to act immorally

questions.feedback_correct: Glaucon is not making a psychological claim about how temptation overcomes virtue. He is making a structural claim: the fact that anyone would use the ring shows that justice is practiced only as a means to avoiding consequences, not as an intrinsic good. His point is that if the external incentives vanish, so does just behavior, which means those incentives, not genuine virtue, are doing all the work.

questions.text: According to Plato's account of the soul in Republic II-IV, which three parts make up the soul?

answers.text: Memory, imagination, and will
Reason, spirit (thumos), and appetite
Wisdom, courage, and self-control
Intellect, emotion, and instinct

questions.feedback_correct: Plato's tripartite soul consists of reason (logos), which governs and seeks truth; spirit (thumos), the assertive, honor-seeking part that enforces reason's directives; and appetite (epithumia), the desiring part that seeks physical satisfactions. questions.text: Plato defines justice in the soul as:

Ensuring that the appetitive part receives its fair share of satisfaction alongside reason and spirit
The complete suppression of appetite so that reason can operate without interference
Each part of the soul performing its proper function, with reason governing spirit and appetite

questions.feedback_correct: For Plato, justice is the harmony that results when each soul-part does what it is suited to do: reason rules, spirit supports reason's governance, and appetite is directed, not destroyed, by reason's guidance. quizzes.title: Week 13 Reading Quiz: Mill, Utilitarianism Chapter II
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Mill's Utilitarianism, Chapter II.

questions.text: According to Mill, the Greatest Happiness Principle holds that actions are right in proportion as they:

answers.text: Tend to promote happiness, wrong as they tend to produce the reverse of happiness
Conform to duties established by reason prior to experience
Benefit the person performing them as well as society at large
Express the will of a rational and benevolent God

questions.feedback_correct: Mill states the Principle of Utility directly in Chapter II: rightness is proportional to the tendency to promote happiness; wrongness to the tendency to produce unhappiness. The principle is consequentialist (about outcomes, not duties), secular (not grounded in God's will), and impartial (not limited to the agent's own benefit).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Mill states the Principle of Utility directly in Chapter II: rightness is proportional to the tendency to promote happiness; wrongness to the tendency to produce unhappiness. The principle is consequentialist (about outcomes, not duties), secular (not grounded in God's will), and impartial (not limited to the agent's own benefit).

questions.text: Mill distinguishes between higher and lower pleasures primarily to respond to which objection?

answers.text: That the Principle of Utility conflicts with traditional religious morality
That utilitarianism cannot explain why we should care about strangers
That utilitarianism requires impossible calculations about future consequences
That utilitarianism reduces morality to a level no better than animal gratification

questions.feedback_correct: The objection that utilitarianism is "a doctrine worthy only of swine" (since it makes pleasure the good, and pigs experience pleasure) is the one Mill directly addresses with the higher/lower distinction. If there are qualitatively superior pleasures that only beings with developed faculties can appreciate, then identifying the good with pleasure does not reduce the human to the animal.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The objection that utilitarianism is "a doctrine worthy only of swine" (since it makes pleasure the good, and pigs experience pleasure) is the one Mill directly addresses with the higher/lower distinction. If there are qualitatively superior pleasures that only beings with developed faculties can appreciate, then identifying the good with pleasure does not reduce the human to the animal.

questions.text: How does Mill propose to determine which pleasures are "higher"?

answers.text: By measuring them with Bentham's hedonic calculus across seven dimensions
By the consistent preferences of those who have experienced both kinds of pleasure
By measuring the duration and intensity of the pleasure produced
By consulting religious authorities about which activities ennoble the soul

questions.feedback_correct: Mill's empirical criterion is the verdict of competent judges, people who have actually experienced both intellectual and purely sensory pleasures. Their consistent preference for the former is evidence that those pleasures are genuinely superior in quality, not merely different. This is not Bentham's calculus, not a matter of measuring duration or intensity, and not a religious appeal, it is a qualitative judgment based on comparative experience.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Mill's empirical criterion is the verdict of competent judges, people who have actually experienced both intellectual and purely sensory pleasures. Their consistent preference for the former is evidence that those pleasures are genuinely superior in quality, not merely different. This is not Bentham's calculus, not a matter of measuring duration or intensity, and not a religious appeal, it is a qualitative judgment based on comparative experience.

questions.text: Which of the following scenarios best illustrates the "justice problem" for act utilitarianism?

answers.text: A judge sentences an innocent person because doing so will prevent a riot that would kill five people
A student spends money on a concert ticket rather than donating to a charity that would save lives
A factory closes because its pollution harms more people than the factory employs
A government taxes wealthy citizens to fund hospitals that help the poor

questions.feedback_correct: The justice problem arises when the utilitarian calculus appears to justify punishing or harming an innocent person because doing so produces better aggregate outcomes. This scenario captures it exactly: the calculation (one life sacrificed, five saved) seems to favor the unjust action. The other scenarios all involve genuine tradeoffs without the specific injustice of treating an innocent person as a means to a social benefit.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The justice problem arises when the utilitarian calculus appears to justify punishing or harming an innocent person because doing so produces better aggregate outcomes. This scenario captures it exactly: the calculation (one life sacrificed, five saved) seems to favor the unjust action. The other scenarios all involve genuine tradeoffs without the specific injustice of treating an innocent person as a means to a social benefit.

questions.text: Mill responds to the objection that utilitarianism is too demanding by arguing that:

answers.text: The Principle of Utility applies only to governments and large institutions, not to individuals
Most people will never face moral situations complex enough to require full utilitarian calculations
It is always acceptable to approximate the utilitarian calculus rather than compute it precisely
Accumulated human experience has already encoded utilitarian wisdom into the ordinary moral rules we follow

questions.feedback_correct: Mill's response moves toward rule utilitarianism: he argues that our inherited moral rules (honesty, promise-keeping, helping others) are the compressed result of generations of human experience discovering what behaviors, practiced reliably, actually promote welfare. We don't need to recalculate from scratch, the rules have already done that work. He is not narrowing the theory's scope to institutions or accepting approximation as a workaround.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Mill's response moves toward rule utilitarianism: he argues that our inherited moral rules (honesty, promise-keeping, helping others) are the compressed result of generations of human experience discovering what behaviors, practiced reliably, actually promote welfare. We don't need to recalculate from scratch, the rules have already done that work. He is not narrowing the theory's scope to institutions or accepting approximation as a workaround.

questions.text: Mill's famous line "It is better to be Socrates dissatisfied than a fool satisfied" illustrates which of his central claims?

answers.text: Intellectual people are happier on balance than those who pursue pleasure
Dissatisfaction is itself a form of happiness when it arises from a life well lived
A small amount of higher pleasure is worth more than a large amount of lower pleasure, even at the cost of some unhappiness
Wisdom, not pleasure, is the ultimate goal of the moral life

questions.feedback_correct: The line is Mill's argument for the qualitative superiority of higher pleasures. Socrates, capable of higher pleasures, experiences more genuine value in his life even if he is often dissatisfied, because the pleasures he does experience are of a higher kind. The "fool" is fully satisfied by lower pleasures but has never accessed the qualitatively superior ones. The claim is about the value of the kind of pleasure, not that dissatisfaction is good or that wisdom replaces pleasure as the goal.

Socrates, capable of higher pleasures, experiences more genuine value in his life even if he is often dissatisfied, because the pleasures he does experience are of a higher kind. The "fool" is fully satisfied by lower pleasures but has never accessed the qualitatively superior ones. The claim is about the value of the kind of pleasure, not that dissatisfaction is good or that wisdom replaces pleasure as the goal.

quizzes.title: Week 14 Reading Quiz: Kant, Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Kant's Groundwork of the Metaphysics of Morals, Book II selections.

questions.text: Kant opens the Groundwork by declaring that only one thing is "good without limitation." What is it?

answers.text: A good will
Happiness, when shared equally among all people
Justice, understood as fairness in the distribution of goods
Rational knowledge of the natural world

questions.feedback_correct: Kant's opening claim is that a good will is the only unconditional good. Everything else, intelligence, courage, health, even happiness, is good only conditionally, depending on the will that directs it. A clever person can be a clever villain; a courageous person can be courageously evil. But a will that acts from duty, governed by reason, is good without qualification.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Kant's opening claim is that a good will is the only unconditional good. Everything else, intelligence, courage, health, even happiness, is good only conditionally, depending on the will that directs it. A clever person can be a clever villain; a courageous person can be courageously evil. But a will that acts from duty, governed by reason, is good without qualification.

questions.text: Kant distinguishes between acting "in conformity with duty" and acting "from duty." Which of the following correctly describes the difference?

answers.text: Acting in conformity with duty means following the law; acting from duty means following one's own moral principles
Acting from duty requires feeling virtuous; acting in conformity with duty requires no particular feeling
Acting in conformity with duty applies to public behavior; acting from duty applies to private choices
Acting from duty means doing the right thing because you recognize it as required by moral law; acting in conformity with duty means doing the right thing for other reasons, such as personal benefit

questions.feedback_correct: For Kant, moral worth depends on the motivation for an action, not just the action itself. A merchant who is honest because honesty is good for business acts in conformity with duty but not from it. A person who tells a painful truth at personal cost because honesty is morally required acts from duty. Only the latter has genuine moral worth in Kant's framework.
questions.feedback_incorrect: For Kant, moral worth depends on the motivation for an action, not just the action itself. A merchant who is honest because honesty is good for business acts in conformity with duty but not from it. A person who tells a painful truth at personal cost because honesty is morally required acts from duty. Only the latter has genuine moral worth in Kant's framework.

questions.text: What is a "maxim" in Kant's moral philosophy?

answers.text: The personal principle or rule underlying a specific action
The intended consequence of an action, considered from the actor's point of view
A general proverb about good behavior passed down through cultural tradition
A universal moral law established by reason and binding on all rational beings

questions.feedback_correct: A maxim is the principle on which an agent acts in a given situation. When someone lies to avoid embarrassment, their maxim might be: "When telling the truth is uncomfortable, I will lie." The categorical imperative tests whether such a maxim can be universalized without contradiction. Maxims are personal principles, not universal laws already established, and not statements about consequences.
questions.feedback_incorrect: A maxim is the principle on which an agent acts in a given situation. When someone lies to avoid embarrassment, their maxim might be: "When telling the truth is uncomfortable, I will lie." The categorical imperative tests whether such a maxim can be universalized without contradiction. Maxims are personal principles, not universal laws already established, and not statements about consequences.

questions.text: Kant's Formula of Universal Law requires that you "act only according to that maxim whereby you can at the same time will that it should become a universal law." Applying this test, why is making a false promise impermissible?

answers.text: Because false promises cause more unhappiness than honest ones across all cases
Because the person deceived would be made unhappy, and everyone's happiness must count equally
Because false promises violate a divine commandment that has force independent of reason
Because universalizing the maxim of false promising would destroy the institution of promising itself, on which the false promise relies

questions.feedback_correct: The universalizability test reveals a logical contradiction: if everyone made false promises whenever convenient, no one would believe promises anymore. The very practice of promising, which the false promiser is exploiting, would cease to function. This is different from a utilitarian calculation about aggregate unhappiness. Kant's argument is about internal consistency, not consequences.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The universalizability test reveals a logical contradiction: if everyone made false promises whenever convenient, no one would believe promises anymore. The very practice of promising, which the false promiser is exploiting, would cease to function. This is different from a utilitarian calculation about aggregate unhappiness. Kant's argument is about internal consistency, not consequences.

questions.text: The Formula of Humanity states that we must treat persons "never as a means only." What does it mean to treat someone as a means only?

answers.text: To pay someone for their labor without also caring about their personal wellbeing
To bypass a person's rational agency by deceiving or coercing them in order to achieve your own ends
To value a person primarily for their social role or economic contribution
To treat a person as less intelligent or capable than they actually are

questions.feedback_correct: Treating someone as a means only means using them as an instrument while ignoring or overriding their status as a rational agent capable of making their own decisions. Deception bypasses rational agency because the deceived person cannot give genuine informed consent. Coercion forces a person to act against their own judgment. Paying for labor is not treating someone as a means "only" as long as their agency and rights are respected.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Treating someone as a means only means using them as an instrument while ignoring or overriding their status as a rational agent capable of making their own decisions. Deception bypasses rational agency because the deceived person cannot give genuine informed consent. Coercion forces a person to act against their own judgment. Paying for labor is not treating someone as a means "only" as long as their agency and rights are respected.

questions.text: What is the "Kingdom of Ends" in Kant's moral philosophy?

answers.text: The political community that will exist once all nations adopt utilitarian governance
The ideal state described in Plato's Republic, where philosophers rule and justice is perfectly realized
A possible moral community in which every rational being is treated both as a subject of the moral law and as a co-legislator of it
Heaven, understood as the reward for those who have lived according to duty

questions.feedback_correct: The Kingdom of Ends is Kant's image of the moral community: a world in which every rational being is an end in themselves and also a legislator of the universal moral law they all share. It is not a political program, not Plato's Republic, and not a religious afterlife. It is a regulative ideal, a picture of what morality is aiming at.

quizzes.title: Week 15 Reading Quiz: Aristotle, Nicomachean Ethics Books I & II
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Aristotle's Nicomachean Ethics, Books I & II.

questions.text: Aristotle opens the Nicomachean Ethics by arguing that every action and pursuit aims at some good. What does he call the highest good, the good we seek for its own sake and not for the sake of anything further?

answers.text: Virtue (arete)
Practical wisdom (phronesis)
Eudaimonia (happiness or flourishing)
Pleasure (hedone)

questions.feedback_correct: Aristotle argues that there must be some final end to which all our actions ultimately aim, something desired for its own sake alone. He identifies this as eudaimonia, usually translated as happiness or flourishing. Virtue is the means by which eudaimonia is achieved, not the end itself. Pleasure is what many people mistake for eudaimonia. Practical wisdom is an intellectual virtue that guides virtuous action.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Aristotle argues that there must be some final end to which all our actions ultimately aim, something desired for its own sake alone. He identifies this as eudaimonia, usually translated as happiness or flourishing. Virtue is the means by which eudaimonia is achieved, not the end itself. Pleasure is what many people mistake for eudaimonia. Practical wisdom is an intellectual virtue that guides virtuous action.

questions.text: Aristotle's Function Argument identifies the good for human beings as "the activity of the soul in accordance with virtue." What is distinctive about human beings that leads to this conclusion?

answers.text: Human beings have the capacity for rational activity, which distinguishes them from other living things
Human beings are capable of experiencing a wider range of pleasures than other animals
Human beings have immortal souls that connect them to a higher realm
Human beings are social animals who depend on one another for survival

questions.feedback_correct: The Function Argument works by identifying what is distinctive about human beings as a kind of living thing. Plants share nutrition and growth; animals share perception and movement. What is uniquely human is rational activity. Therefore, excellent human activity, what constitutes the good for human beings, is the excellent exercise of rational capacity. This is why virtue, which perfects rational activity, is central to eudaimonia.

Plants share nutrition and growth; animals share perception and movement. What is uniquely human is rational activity. Therefore, excellent human activity, what constitutes the good for human beings, is the excellent exercise of rational capacity. This is why virtue, which perfects rational activity, is central to eudaimonia.

questions.text: Aristotle says that moral virtues are acquired through habituation. What does he mean?

answers.text: We are born with natural virtuous tendencies that need only to be refined by education
We acquire virtue by studying moral philosophy and applying its principles to our behavior
We develop virtue by imitating the perfectly virtuous person described in philosophical texts
We become virtuous by repeatedly performing virtuous actions until the disposition becomes stable and natural

questions.feedback_correct: Aristotle's central claim in Book II is that moral virtues are not innate and not acquired by knowledge alone. We become courageous by doing courageous things, just by doing just things, temperate by doing temperate things. Repeated practice forms stable dispositions of character, hexeis, that eventually make virtuous action natural and even pleasurable. This is different from simply knowing what virtue is or imitating an abstract ideal.

This is different from simply knowing what virtue is or imitating an abstract ideal.

questions.text: According to Aristotle's doctrine of the mean, what is the relationship between a virtue and the vices on either side of it?

answers.text: A virtue is the complete suppression of the corresponding vices
A virtue is the mean between a vice of excess and a vice of deficiency, relative to the person and situation
A virtue is a compromise between two morally acceptable extremes
A virtue is the exact midpoint between two extremes when measured mathematically

questions.feedback_correct: The doctrine of the mean holds that each virtue is the appropriate response between too much (excess) and too little (deficiency), where "appropriate" is relative to the person and the situation, not a fixed arithmetic middle. Courage is the mean between recklessness (excess) and cowardice (deficiency), but what counts as the courageous response differs for a soldier in battle and a student making a difficult argument in class. The mean is not mathematical and not a compromise between acceptable options.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The doctrine of the mean holds that each virtue is the appropriate response between too much (excess) and too little (deficiency), where "appropriate" is relative to the person and the situation, not a fixed arithmetic middle. Courage is the mean between recklessness (excess) and cowardice (deficiency), but what counts as the courageous response differs for a soldier in battle and a student making a difficult argument in class. The mean is not mathematical and not a compromise between acceptable options.

questions.text: What distinguishes a continent person from a truly virtuous person in Aristotle's account?

answers.text: The continent person acts rightly but against the pull of opposing desires; the virtuous person acts rightly with desires and reason aligned
The continent person knows the moral rules; the virtuous person has internalized them
The continent person acts from duty; the virtuous person acts from inclination
The continent person is virtuous in private but not in public; the virtuous person is consistent in all contexts

questions.feedback_correct: Continence is the condition of someone who acts rightly while experiencing the ongoing pull of contrary desires. The continent person is better than the vicious person but not yet fully virtuous. Full virtue requires not merely doing the right thing but having character so well-formed that reason and emotion are aligned: the virtuous person feels the right emotions, perceives the situation correctly, and acts accordingly without internal conflict.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Continence is the condition of someone who acts rightly while experiencing the ongoing pull of contrary desires. The continent person is better than the vicious person but not yet fully virtuous. Full virtue requires not merely doing the right thing but having character so well-formed that reason and emotion are aligned: the virtuous person feels the right emotions, perceives the situation correctly, and acts accordingly without internal conflict.

questions.text: Which of the following best describes the role of practical wisdom (phronesis) in Aristotle's account of virtue?

answers.text: It is the highest virtue, whose possession automatically confers all other virtues
It is the virtue concerned specifically with the fair distribution of goods among people in a community
It is the capacity for theoretical knowledge of moral philosophy, which guides action
It is the virtue of deliberating well and perceiving what a particular situation requires, unifying all the moral virtues

questions.feedback_correct: Practical wisdom is the intellectual virtue that governs all the moral virtues. It is not theoretical knowledge of ethics but a practical, perceptual, and deliberative capacity: the ability to see what a situation morally requires and to bring the right virtues to bear in the right way. Without practical wisdom, the other virtues are incomplete, a person may have courageous dispositions but lack the judgment to see how courage applies in a novel situation.

quizzes.description: 6 questions on Hobbes's Leviathan, Chapters 11, 13-14, and 17.

questions.text: According to Hobbes in Leviathan I.13, what is the condition of human beings in the "state of nature"?

answers.text: A golden age of simple cooperation, before the corrupting influence of government
A peaceful pastoral state in which natural instincts promote harmony
A condition of mild competition regulated by unwritten natural customs
A condition of war of every man against every man, with no security and no productive life

questions.feedback_correct: Hobbes argues that without a common power to overawe everyone, the state of nature is one of universal war, not a series of battles, but a persistent condition of mutual threat and insecurity. In it, there is no industry, no arts, no letters, no society, and life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short" (Leviathan, ch. 13).
questions.feedback_incorrect: Hobbes argues that without a common power to overawe everyone, the state of nature is one of universal war, not a series of battles, but a persistent condition of mutual threat and insecurity. In it, there is no industry, no arts, no letters, no society, and life is "solitary, poor, nasty, brutish, and short" (Leviathan, ch. 13).

questions.text: Hobbes begins his argument with the claim that human beings are naturally equal. What does he mean by this, and why does it matter?

answers.text: People have roughly equal strength and cunning, so no one is safe from attack, which produces mutual fear and conflict
People have equal natural rights that must be protected by a democratic government
People's desires are equally valid, so no single vision of the good life can be imposed
People are morally equal, so no one has the right to govern others without consent

questions.feedback_correct: Hobbes's equality is a claim about power, not moral status: even the weakest person can kill the strongest with sufficient cunning or allies. From this rough equality comes equality of hope in achieving one's goals, which produces competition; and from competition comes mutual fear (diffidence), which produces preemptive conflict.

From this rough equality comes equality of hope in achieving one's goals, which produces competition; and from competition comes mutual fear (diffidence), which produces preemptive conflict.

questions.text: Hobbes identifies three principal causes of conflict in the state of nature. Which of the following correctly lists them?

answers.text: Greed, envy, and pride
Hunger, desire, and ambition
Competition, diffidence, and glory
Fear, ignorance, and inequality

questions.feedback_correct: Hobbes explicitly names competition (quarreling over scarce goods), diffidence (preemptive self-defense driven by mutual distrust), and glory (the desire for reputation and recognition through dominance) as the three sources of conflict that make the state of nature a state of war.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Hobbes explicitly names competition (quarreling over scarce goods), diffidence (preemptive self-defense driven by mutual distrust), and glory (the desire for reputation and recognition through dominance) as the three sources of conflict that make the state of nature a state of war.

questions.text: What is Hobbes's right of nature (jus naturale), and what limits it?

answers.text: The right to be treated fairly by others; limited by the duty to treat others fairly in return
The right to use any means necessary to preserve one's own life; limited in practice only by one's power to exercise it
The right to form political communities; limited by the need for unanimous consent
The right to acquire property; limited by the principle of equal shares

questions.feedback_correct: In the state of nature, the right of nature is the unlimited liberty each person has to do whatever they judge necessary for self-preservation. It is not morally limited by duties to others, in the state of nature, there is no injustice, because there is no law. It is limited only by one's actual power.
questions.feedback_incorrect: In the state of nature, the right of nature is the unlimited liberty each person has to do whatever they judge necessary for self-preservation. It is not morally limited by duties to others, in the state of nature, there is no injustice, because there is no law. It is limited only by one's actual power.

questions.text: Why does Hobbes reject the idea of a summum bonum (highest good) as the foundation of political life?

answers.text: He believes people naturally disagree about what is good, so there is no shared final end that politics can be organized around
He believes the highest good is happiness, but happiness is too subjective to legislate
He accepts that there is a highest good, but argues it can only be achieved after death
He believes God, not reason, determines the highest good, so it cannot be known through philosophy

questions.feedback_correct: Hobbes explicitly denies that there is any finis ultimus (utmost aim) or summum bonum as described by ancient philosophers. Human beings pursue different things, and their desires are endless rather than oriented toward a shared final end. This means politics cannot be grounded in a vision of the good life; it must instead be grounded in something everyone shares, the desire to avoid death.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Hobbes explicitly denies that there is any finis ultimus (utmost aim) or summum bonum as described by ancient philosophers. Human beings pursue different things, and their desires are endless rather than oriented toward a shared final end. This means politics cannot be grounded in a vision of the good life; it must instead be grounded in something everyone shares, the desire to avoid death.

questions.text: What is the summum malum (greatest evil) in Hobbes's framework, and why does it serve as the foundation of political authority?

answers.text: Injustice; because everyone naturally desires justice and recognizes injustice as harmful
Poverty; because material deprivation prevents any kind of meaningful life
Tyranny; because unlimited government is worse than the state of nature
Violent, premature death; because the desire to avoid death is universal and can ground a political agreement even among people who disagree about the good

questions.feedback_correct: Hobbes argues that although people disagree about the good life, they universally share the desire to avoid violent death. This shared aversion is the one thing that can ground a rational social contract across people with very different values and desires. The sovereign's primary job is therefore not to make citizens virtuous or happy, but to keep them alive and secure.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Hobbes argues that although people disagree about the good life, they universally share the desire to avoid violent death. This shared aversion is the one thing that can ground a rational social contract across people with very different values and desires. The sovereign's primary job is therefore not to make citizens virtuous or happy, but to keep them alive and secure.
