quizzes.title: Week 17 Reading Quiz: Aristotle, Politics I.1-2
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Aristotle's Politics, Book I, Chapters 1-2.

questions.text: How does Aristotle open the Politics, and what does this opening reveal about his method?

answers.text: With a definition of justice, showing that ethics must precede politics
With a history of Greek cities, showing that his method is empirical and historical
With a refutation of Plato, showing that politics cannot be based on abstract philosophy
With the claim that every community aims at some good, showing that his political philosophy is teleological, organized around purposes and ends

questions.feedback_correct: Aristotle opens: "Every polis is a community of some kind, and every community is established with a view to some good." This reveals the teleological character of his political philosophy: communities exist for purposes, and the quality of a community is measured by how well it achieves its characteristic purpose. The highest community, the polis, aims at the highest good.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Aristotle opens: "Every polis is a community of some kind, and every community is established with a view to some good." This reveals the teleological character of his political philosophy: communities exist for purposes, and the quality of a community is measured by how well it achieves its characteristic purpose. The highest community, the polis, aims at the highest good.

questions.text: What does Aristotle mean when he says man is by nature a zōon politikon, a "political animal"?

answers.text: That political community is the natural completion of human development, the condition in which human capacities are fully exercised
That human beings are naturally aggressive and competitive, and therefore need political control
That human beings formed political communities very early in their evolutionary history
That human beings are naturally drawn to political power and seek to govern others

questions.feedback_correct: For Aristotle, "by nature" means teleologically, the polis is the context in which human nature reaches its telos (its complete development). Man is a political animal not because he is aggressive or power-seeking, but because the full exercise of his distinctively human capacities, reasoned speech, deliberation about justice, requires political community.
questions.feedback_incorrect: For Aristotle, "by nature" means teleologically, the polis is the context in which human nature reaches its telos (its complete development). Man is a political animal not because he is aggressive or power-seeking, but because the full exercise of his distinctively human capacities, reasoned speech, deliberation about justice, requires political community.

questions.text: Aristotle argues that man is more political than bees or other social animals. What is his reason?

answers.text: Human beings form larger and more organized groups than other social animals
Human beings are more dependent on one another for survival than any other species
Human beings have language (logos) and can reason about and discuss good and evil, just and unjust, not merely signal pleasure and pain
Human beings are the only animals who choose their leaders through deliberate selection

questions.feedback_correct: Aristotle distinguishes phōnē (voice, which other animals have) from logos (speech-reason, which is distinctively human). Other animals can signal pleasure and pain. Only human beings can deliberate about what is good and just, and this capacity for reasoned deliberation about the good is what makes a genuine political community (not just a herd) possible and what makes human beings political animals in the fullest sense.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Aristotle distinguishes phōnē (voice, which other animals have) from logos (speech-reason, which is distinctively human). Other animals can signal pleasure and pain. Only human beings can deliberate about what is good and just, and this capacity for reasoned deliberation about the good is what makes a genuine political community (not just a herd) possible and what makes human beings political animals in the fullest sense.

questions.text: Aristotle describes a progression from household to village to polis. What is the key difference between the village and the polis?

answers.text: The village is governed by elected officials; the polis is governed by a king
The village is based on kinship; the polis is based on a voluntary social contract
The village is ruled by custom; the polis is ruled by written law
The village exists for daily needs and survival; the polis comes into being for living but exists for the sake of the good life (eudaimonia)

questions.feedback_correct: Aristotle's famous formulation: "The polis comes into being for the sake of living, but it exists for the sake of the good life." The village, like the household, addresses material and survival needs. The polis is the self-sufficient community in which human beings can not only survive but genuinely flourish, exercising their rational, political, artistic, and philosophical capacities fully.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Aristotle's famous formulation: "The polis comes into being for the sake of living, but it exists for the sake of the good life." The village, like the household, addresses material and survival needs. The polis is the self-sufficient community in which human beings can not only survive but genuinely flourish, exercising their rational, political, artistic, and philosophical capacities fully.

questions.text: What does Aristotle mean by saying "the polis is prior by nature to the individual"?

answers.text: Cities are older than individuals historically, since cities existed before any living person
In terms of natural completion and purpose, the individual reaches full development only within the polis, just as a hand separated from a body is no longer fully a hand
Political authority exists before individual rights and is the source of those rights
The interests of the city always override the interests of individuals legally

questions.feedback_correct: Aristotle's claim is teleological, not chronological or legal. Just as a hand is only truly a hand when it performs its function as part of a body, a human being is only fully human when exercising their distinctively human capacities, which requires the polis. The individual is not prior to the community in the sense of being more complete; the community is what makes individual completion possible.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Aristotle's claim is teleological, not chronological or legal. Just as a hand is only truly a hand when it performs its function as part of a body, a human being is only fully human when exercising their distinctively human capacities, which requires the polis. The individual is not prior to the community in the sense of being more complete; the community is what makes individual completion possible.

questions.text: Which of the following best captures the deepest disagreement between Aristotle and Hobbes about political community?

answers.text: Aristotle thinks political community is natural and aimed at the good life; Hobbes thinks it is an artificial construction aimed at preventing violent death
Aristotle believes in democracy; Hobbes believes in monarchy
Aristotle thinks philosophy is irrelevant to politics; Hobbes thinks philosophy is the foundation of good government
Aristotle believes the individual has natural rights; Hobbes believes the sovereign creates all rights

questions.feedback_correct: The root disagreement is about human nature and the purpose of political life. For Aristotle, human beings are by nature political animals, and the polis exists to enable the good life, eudaimonia. For Hobbes, human beings are by nature isolated individuals, and political community is an artificial remedy for the terror of the state of nature, aimed not at flourishing but at security. Every other difference between them flows from this fundamental disagreement.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The root disagreement is about human nature and the purpose of political life. For Aristotle, human beings are by nature political animals, and the polis exists to enable the good life, eudaimonia. For Hobbes, human beings are by nature isolated individuals, and political community is an artificial remedy for the terror of the state of nature, aimed not at flourishing but at security. Every other difference between them flows from this fundamental disagreement.

quizzes.title: Week 18 Reading Quiz: Plato, Republic VI & VII
quizzes.description: 6 questions on Plato's Republic VI (509d-511e) and VII (514a-521b).

questions.text: In the Divided Line (Republic VI, 509d-511e), what is the primary division that Plato draws, and what corresponds to each side?

answers.text: A division between the past and the future; the past corresponds to memory, the future to imagination
A division between the body and the soul; the body corresponds to desire and the soul corresponds to reason
A division between Greek and barbarian thought; Greek thought is rational and barbarian thought is merely conventional
A division between the visible and the intelligible realms; the visible realm corresponds to opinion and the intelligible realm corresponds to knowledge

questions.feedback_correct: The Divided Line's primary division is between the visible realm (to horaton), the world of sensory perception, corresponding to doxa (opinion), and the intelligible realm (to noēton), the world grasped by intellect, corresponding to epistēmē (knowledge). The line is then divided again within each half to give four levels total.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The Divided Line's primary division is between the visible realm (to horaton), the world of sensory perception, corresponding to doxa (opinion), and the intelligible realm (to noēton), the world grasped by intellect, corresponding to epistēmē (knowledge). The line is then divided again within each half to give four levels total.

questions.text: What does the Form of the Good represent in Plato's Divided Line, and how does he compare it to the sun?

answers.text: The Form of the Good is the source of both the being of all other Forms and their knowability, just as the sun is the source of both the existence and the visibility of things in the visible realm
The Form of the Good is the highest moral law, which Plato compares to the sun because both can be blinding if approached directly
The Form of the Good is unknowable, which Plato compares to the sun because one can never look directly at the sun
The Form of the Good is the most beautiful Form, which Plato compares to the sun because beauty radiates outward like sunlight

questions.feedback_correct: Plato writes that the Form of the Good provides the things that are known with both their being and their being known (Republic VI, 509b). Just as the sun causes visible things to exist and grow, and also provides the light by which they are seen, so the Form of the Good grounds both the being of the intelligible Forms and the capacity of the mind to grasp them.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Plato writes that the Form of the Good provides the things that are known with both their being and their being known (Republic VI, 509b). Just as the sun causes visible things to exist and grow, and also provides the light by which they are seen, so the Form of the Good grounds both the being of the intelligible Forms and the capacity of the mind to grasp them.

questions.text: In the Allegory of the Cave, what do the shadows on the cave wall represent, and what do the prisoners who study them represent?

answers.text: The shadows represent mathematical truths; the prisoners represent mathematicians
The shadows represent the Forms; the prisoners represent philosophers who have not yet seen the Good
The shadows represent political speeches; the prisoners represent citizens who are governed by rhetoric rather than reason
The shadows represent images and appearances, the lowest level of the visible realm; the prisoners represent people who take conventional opinion and sensory appearances for reality

questions.feedback_correct: The shadows are the lowest level of the Divided Line, eikasia, images and appearances. The prisoners who name and study them represent the condition of people who take the world of conventional opinion and unreflective sensory experience as the whole of reality, without questioning whether what they perceive is the truth.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The shadows are the lowest level of the Divided Line, eikasia, images and appearances. The prisoners who name and study them represent the condition of people who take the world of conventional opinion and unreflective sensory experience as the whole of reality, without questioning whether what they perceive is the truth.

questions.text: Plato says philosophical education is not "putting knowledge into souls that lack it" but rather a "turning of the whole soul." What does he mean?

answers.text: The capacity for knowledge is already present in every soul; philosophical education reorients the whole person, their desires, attention, and values, from the shadows toward the light
Only the rational part of the soul can be educated; the spirited and appetitive parts must simply be suppressed
Philosophy requires erasing all prior knowledge before new knowledge can be received
Philosophical education is primarily about memorizing the arguments of great philosophers

questions.feedback_correct: Plato's point is that philosophical education is a transformation of character, not merely an accumulation of information. The capacity to learn is present in everyone (Republic VII, 518c). What is needed is the turning of the whole soul, a reorientation of one's entire being toward truth and the Good, rather than toward the shadows of convention and opinion.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Plato's point is that philosophical education is a transformation of character, not merely an accumulation of information. The capacity to learn is present in everyone (Republic VII, 518c). What is needed is the turning of the whole soul, a reorientation of one's entire being toward truth and the Good, rather than toward the shadows of convention and opinion.

questions.text: Why must the philosopher who has escaped the cave and seen the sun return to the cave? What are Plato's reasons?

answers.text: Because seeing the sun is so painful that the philosopher prefers the cave's familiar darkness
Because the other prisoners need to be forcibly removed from the cave, which requires the philosopher's physical return
Because the philosopher owes a debt to the community that educated them, and because only someone who has seen the Good is fitted to govern justly
Because knowledge of the Forms is only stable when regularly confirmed by contrast with the cave's shadows

questions.feedback_correct: Plato gives two reasons for the return. First, justice: the philosopher was educated by the city and owes it the service of governance (Republic VII, 520b). Second, fitness: only the philosopher who has seen the Form of the Good genuinely knows what is good for the city and its citizens. Rulers who have not left the cave will govern in the interest of shadows, money, reputation, power, rather than genuine justice and flourishing.
questions.feedback_incorrect: Plato gives two reasons for the return. First, justice: the philosopher was educated by the city and owes it the service of governance (Republic VII, 520b). Second, fitness: only the philosopher who has seen the Form of the Good genuinely knows what is good for the city and its citizens. Rulers who have not left the cave will govern in the interest of shadows, money, reputation, power, rather than genuine justice and flourishing.

questions.text: The prisoner who returns to the cave is mocked, disoriented, and threatened with death. What does this part of the Allegory represent, and what does it suggest about Socrates?

answers.text: It represents the difficulty of adjusting to physical darkness after bright sunlight, a purely optical phenomenon
It represents the reception of philosophical truth in a community that has not left the cave, including the fate of Socrates, who was mocked, put on trial, and executed for his philosophical activity
It represents Plato's belief that philosophers should never return to political life, since the danger is too great
It represents the philosopher's intellectual failure to communicate truth to ordinary people, suggesting that philosophy should remain private

questions.feedback_correct: The return to the cave is a portrait of the philosopher's condition in any real political community, including Athens. The prisoner who returns and can no longer navigate the shadows well is mocked; if the others could, they would kill him. This is the fate of Socrates: the man who left the cave of Athenian conventional opinion and returned to question it was tried and executed. The Allegory does not conclude that Socrates was wrong; it concludes that the cave's inhabitants are.
questions.feedback_incorrect: The return to the cave is a portrait of the philosopher's condition in any real political community, including Athens. The prisoner who returns and can no longer navigate the shadows well is mocked; if the others could, they would kill him. This is the fate of Socrates: the man who left the cave of Athenian conventional opinion and returned to question it was tried and executed. The Allegory does not conclude that Socrates was wrong; it concludes that the cave's inhabitants are.
